print_output.notes: Printing variables, expressions (print(2 + 3) vs print('2 + 3')) and f-strings are left to B02 variables/expressions and B03 string_formatting; they should encompass these topics. Quotes inside strings and escaping quotes are left to B03 strings; only \n and \t are taught here because output layout needs them.

running_scripts.notes: statements_run_in_order is environment-agnostic (works in a browser IDE) so it can be core; run_from_terminal is the local-install path. Full traceback reading belongs to B09 debugging/exceptions.

comments.notes: Docstrings are B05; pseudocode-as-comments is B05 pseudocode.

command_line.notes: Only what a Python learner needs (navigation, paths, file management). Linux filesystem, permissions, redirection are out of scope per plan.json. Command-line arguments to scripts are B10 command_line_args.

python_setup.notes: pip and virtual environments belong to tool_pip / third_party_packages in a later batch.

pep8_style.notes: Only layout rules applicable to wave-1 code. Naming conventions (snake_case, UPPER_CASE constants, CapWords classes) should be owned by B02 variables/constants, B05 functions and the OOP batch, encompassing pep8_style.spacing_and_layout.

computer_architecture.notes: Introduced by py4e only; one supplemental topic.

variables.notes: Scope and global variables are B05 scope. a, b = b, a is used in swap_values as a preview; tuple unpacking proper is B06 unpacking. Names-as-references for mutable objects (aliasing) is B06 mutability_aliasing. naming_rules covers the PEP 8 naming conventions B01 deferred here; it is core, so pep8_style.spacing_and_layout (non-core) is neither a prerequisite nor encompassed.

data_types.notes: Only two topics because the type-specific material is owned by integers_floats, booleans, none_type and type_conversion in this batch, and strings by B03. isinstance() and classes-as-types belong to the OOP batch (B11). D2 previews "2" + "3" joining strings; B03 string_concatenation owns concatenation and should encompass data_types.types_decide_operations.

integers_floats.notes: round() and abs() are taught here because floats need them early; B05 builtin_functions should reference rather than re-teach them. Binary representation, epsilon methods and the decimal module are B14 floating_point_precision; math module functions are B13 math_module.

arithmetic_operators.notes: Augmented assignment (+= etc.) is owned by variables.update_with_own_value. Divisibility tests with if are B04 conditionals, which should encompass modulo_patterns. ^ is mentioned only as 'not power'; bitwise operators are B14 binary_bitwise.

expressions.notes: print(2 + 3) vs print('2 + 3') (deferred from B01 print_output) is expressions.evaluate_expressions KP1. Conditional expressions (x if c else y) are B04.

constants.notes: Global constants used inside functions belong to B05 scope; math.pi etc. to B13 math_module; Enum to B11 enums.

none_type.notes: Functions that return None implicitly (and print() returning None) belong to B05 return_values, which should encompass none_type.none_value. 'is' vs '==' on mutable objects belongs to B06 mutability_aliasing; check_for_none only covers None and the literal warning.

type_conversion.notes: bool() conversion is booleans.truthiness. Handling ValueError with try/except is B09 exceptions (cs50p 'get an integer' function). str() for building output with + is B03 string_concatenation, which should encompass type_conversion.numbers_and_strings. list()/tuple()/set() conversions belong to B06/B07.

user_input.notes: The concept graph says user_input comes before variables; here it comes after, since storing the answer needs assignment. Re-prompting until valid input is B04 while_loops (sentinel) and B09 exceptions. Input methods like .strip()/.lower() on answers are B03 string_methods.

booleans.notes: Using truthiness in if/while (if name:) is B04 conditionals; summing booleans to count is B04 loop_patterns / B05 builtin_functions.

comparison_operators.notes: String comparison is owned here; B03 should only add case-insensitive comparison via .lower(). The membership operator in is B03 strings / B06 lists. math.isclose is B13 math_module.

logical_operators.notes: All examples are standalone expressions; B04 conditionals uses them in if/while and should encompass logical_operators.and_or_not and combine_conditions.

strings.notes: Iterating over a string with for (traversal, looping and counting characters, py4e 6 / MIT L4) belongs to B04 for_loops / loop_patterns, which run in parallel and should encompass strings.length_and_membership and string_indexing_slicing.index_characters. String equality and ordering are owned by B02 comparison_operators. \n and \t are B01 print_output.newlines_and_tabs (non-core, so encompassed rather than required). Regular expressions are a later batch and can use strings.multiline_and_raw for raw strings.

string_concatenation.notes: Building strings inside loops (accumulating with +=) belongs to B04 loop_patterns, which should encompass join_with_plus. f-strings are the preferred alternative and live in string_formatting.

string_indexing_slicing.notes: Taught before list slicing; B06 list_slicing should list these topics as prerequisites and teach only what differs for lists (slice assignment, copying). Looping over indexes with range(len(s)) is B04.

string_methods.notes: split() returns a list; lists themselves are B06, which should encompass split_into_parts and join_pieces. Loops over split() results and over lines of a file are B04/B10. Alignment methods (center/ljust/rjust/zfill) are covered by f-string specs in string_formatting.width_and_alignment and not given their own topic. partition(), casefold() and dir(str)/help(str) were left out; B05 builtin_functions may add method discovery.

string_formatting.notes: f"{x=}" for debugging belongs to B09 debugging. print(sep=, end=) is B01 print_output.sep_and_end. Format specs for dates are B13 datetime.

string_immutability.notes: One topic, as the evidence is three 'introduced' mentions. The general mutable/immutable distinction and aliasing of lists is B06 mutability_aliasing, which should encompass this topic.

unicode_encoding.notes: Both topics are supplemental. File encodings (open(..., encoding='utf-8')) belong to B10 file_io; bytes from the network to the web batch. A full Caesar cipher over a whole message needs a loop and belongs to B04/B05 practice.

conditionals.notes: Encompasses B02 logical_operators and_or_not/combine_conditions, booleans.truthiness, none_type.check_for_none and arithmetic_operators.modulo_patterns as B02 requested. pass is introduced in if_statement KP4. Case-insensitive comparison of answers (.lower()) is left to B03 string_methods; the in operator for membership tests is B03/B06. try/except around int(input()) is B09 exceptions.

nested_conditionals.notes: flatten_nesting doubles as the 'guard clause' idea; early return as a guard is B05 return_values.

conditional_expressions.notes: One topic: only Helsinki teaches it, but it is core because B07 comprehensions and B08 lambdas use it.

match_statement.notes: Non-core (3 courses, introduced only). Only literal, |, _, capture and guard patterns are taught here; sequence patterns (case [x, y]) belong with B06 lists/unpacking, mapping patterns with B07 dictionaries, class patterns with the OOP batch. Python 3.10+ only. Reconciliation: every snippet was run with Python 3.13; all outputs were correct. Subject assignments and output comments were added to the fragments that lacked them, and the exact SyntaxError for a non-final capture case was quoted.

while_loops.notes: Validation that survives non-numeric input (try/except ValueError) is B09 exceptions. Random secret numbers (random.randint) are B13 random_module; guessing-game examples use a fixed secret. while True + break lives in break_continue.while_true_loops.

for_loops.notes: Without lists (B06) for loops iterate over range and strings only. for_loops.loop_over_characters has pending_prerequisites concept:strings because B03 runs in parallel; if B03 also wrote a 'traverse a string' topic the stitching pass should merge them (one should own it). Looping over lists, enumerate and zip are B06; looping over dict items is B07; looping over file lines is B10.

range_function.notes: range(n) itself is introduced in for_loops.repeat_n_times; this concept owns start/stop/step. list(range(...)), len(range) and membership in a range are B06.

break_continue.notes: loop_else is non-core (taught by no course but a real Python feature). Breaking out of nested loops via a function return is B05 return_values.

nested_loops.notes: grids_and_patterns is non-core because it depends on print_output.sep_and_end (non-core). Nested loops over 2D lists are B07 nested_data_structures; string repetition '#' * n as an alternative to the inner loop is B03 and could encompass grids_and_patterns. Reconciliation: grids_and_patterns is core now that print_output.sep_and_end is core.

loop_patterns.notes: Built-ins sum(), max(), min(), any(), all() that replace these loops are B05 builtin_functions, which should encompass the matching pattern topics. Counting with dictionaries is B07. Guess-and-check / exhaustive enumeration is its own concept (guess_and_check) in a later batch.

iteration.notes: One non-core topic. Custom iterators (__iter__/__next__) are B11 dunder_methods; generators and generator expressions are B08 generators; itertools is B07; enumerate/zip are B06. Reconciliation: iter_and_next promoted to core (generators build on it).

builtin_functions.notes: round()/abs() stay with B02 integers_floats; ord/chr with B03. sum/max/min here use several arguments, ranges and strings only, because lists are in B06 (parallel batch): B06 lists should teach len/sum/max/min of a list and encompass builtin_functions.sum_max_min. any()/all() and summing booleans need iterables of booleans, so they are left to B07 list_comprehensions (generator expressions); sorted() and key= are B06 sorting / B08 higher_order_functions; map/filter are B08; isinstance is B11; divmod/pow were left out (operators // % ** cover them).

functions.notes: Entry is builtin_functions.call_anatomy (calling before defining, as py4e does). Parameters, return values and scope are owned by their own concepts. Functions as objects (passing/storing functions, MIT L8, 100 Days 'functions in a dict') are B08 higher_order_functions; lambda is B08; recursion is B08. try/except inside helper functions (cs50p get_int) is B09.

parameters_arguments.notes: *args/**kwargs and keyword-only/positional-only markers (*, /) are B08 args_kwargs. mutable_default_trap needs lists, so it carries pending_prerequisites concept:lists and concept:mutability_aliasing; if B06 also wrote a mutable-default topic, the stitching pass should keep one. Passing a list into a function and mutating it is B06 mutability_aliasing.

return_values.notes: multiple_return_values teaches only return a, b and unpacking into names; B06 tuples/unpacking should encompass it rather than re-teach it. Breaking out of nested loops via return (B04 note) is a practice item in early_return. Pure vs side-effecting functions as a concept is B08 pure_functions, which can build on decomposition.one_job_per_function.

scope.notes: Enclosing scope, nonlocal and the full LEGB rule belong to B08 closures. Module-level scope across files is B13 modules_imports.

docstrings.notes: Doctests are left to B09 unit_testing. specifications is non-core (MIT, Code in Place only) but feeds abstraction and B09 testing/defensive_programming.

type_hints.notes: Generic container hints (list[int], dict[str, int], tuple[int, int]) belong to B06/B07 when those types are taught; checking hints with mypy is B09 tool_mypy. Reconciliation: container hints (list[int], dict[str, int], tuple[...]) were added as collection_hints; tool_mypy and lib_sqlalchemy.relationships depend on it.

decomposition.notes: Meta-skill taught as three problem-based topics (Parsons, refactoring, fill-in). Function naming conventions (deferred from B01 pep8_style) live in one_job_per_function KP3. Module-level decomposition (own modules) is B13; class-level design is B12.

abstraction.notes: Procedural abstraction only. Data abstraction and the OOP 'abstraction pillar' (bootdev, codecademy, MIT L17) belong to B11/B12.

pseudocode.notes: Only cs50p teaches it, so one non-core topic. Flowcharts (100 Days Day 7) were not given a topic.

computational_thinking.notes: One non-core topic on algorithms (declarative vs imperative, precision, tracing). Its parts decomposition and abstraction have their own topics; guess-and-check, bisection and Newton are B14.

karel_robot.notes: Non-core: needs a Karel world embedded in the platform (Code in Place / Reeborg). Placed after functions, so it serves as practice for defining commands rather than as a first-week entry point.

main_guard.notes: Needs import to show its point, so it has pending_prerequisites concept:modules_imports (B13, a later wave). The plain main() pattern without the guard is core and lives in functions.main_and_helpers, so B09 unit_testing can depend on that if it should not wait for B13.

lists.notes: Looping over lists (deferred by B04) is lists.loop_over_items / loop_over_indexes; they encompass the B04 loop_patterns. split/join (B03 request) are encompassed by lists.text_to_list_and_back, which depends on list_methods.append_build. list(range()), len(range) and list('str') are in membership_and_operators KP4. sum()/min()/max() on lists are B05 builtin_functions, which should encompass lists.loop_over_items. Lists of lists / 2D grids are B07 nested_data_structures (copying.shallow_vs_deep only previews double indexing). Lists as function parameters live in mutability_aliasing.lists_in_functions. random.choice on lists is B13 random_module. Sequence patterns in match (case [x, y]) were not added; B07 or a stitching pass may add them. Reconciliation: len/sum/max/min of a list (the B05/B06 gap) is lists.aggregate_builtins; later topics that apply these built-ins to lists depend on it instead of builtin_functions.sum_max_min.

list_methods.notes: sort()/reverse() are taught in sorting.sort_and_sorted. clear() is mentioned only in mutability_aliasing.lists_in_functions. Using lists as stacks/queues (pop() vs pop(0), deque) is B07 stacks_queues; building lists with comprehensions is B07 list_comprehensions, which should encompass append_build (filter KP).

list_slicing.notes: Builds on B03 string slicing as B03 asked: only what differs for lists (result is a list, slice vs index, slice assignment). Copying with [:] is copying.copy_a_list. slice_assignment is non-core (py4e/Helsinki only). sys.argv[1:] is B10 command_line_args.

tuples.notes: Tuples as dict keys and dict.items() pairs are B07 dictionaries. Returning tuples from functions is unpacking.return_multiple_values. namedtuple is B07 collections_module.

unpacking.notes: B02 variables.swap_values and B03 split_into_parts already preview unpacking; unpack_sequences encompasses them. star_unpacking is non-core and covers *rest and print(*lst) only; *args/**kwargs and ** dict unpacking are B08 args_kwargs. return_multiple_values has pending concept:return_values (B05 runs in parallel); if B05 also wrote a 'return several values' topic, the stitching pass should keep one. Reconciliation: return_multiple_values (duplicate of B05 return_values.multiple_return_values) was replaced by use_returned_tuples, which depends on it.

enumerate_zip.notes: Only 2 courses introduce these, but they are core idioms that replace range(len(...)). dict(zip(keys, values)) is B07 dictionaries; zip(strict=True) and itertools are B07 itertools_module.

mutability_aliasing.notes: lists_in_functions needs def/parameters, so it has pending concept:parameters_arguments (B05 runs in parallel); it includes the mutable default argument gotcha. Aliasing of objects/attributes is the OOP batch (B11). Integer/string interning is deliberately not taught; is is presented as 'only for None'.

copying.notes: shallow_vs_deep is non-core and previews lists of lists, which B07 nested_data_structures owns; it uses `import copy` before B13 modules_imports, as a single memorised line. Copying dicts (dict.copy) is B07.

sorting.notes: key= is taught only with existing functions (len, str.lower). key=lambda and key=<own function> belong to B08 lambda_functions / higher_order_functions, which should encompass sort_tuples_and_keys. Sorting dict items by value is B07 dictionaries (py4e 'sorting a dictionary using tuples'). Sorting algorithms (bubble, merge sort) are a later algorithms batch.

dictionaries.notes: Ten topics: taught by 8/8 courses (deep), and B06 handed over dict(zip()), tuple keys, sorting a dict by value and dict.copy(). Mapping patterns in match (deferred by B04) are in nested_data_structures.match_structure_patterns. Hash table internals are a later batch (hash_maps_internals). Generic hints like dict[str, int] were not given a KP; B09 tool_mypy or a stitching pass may add them. Storing functions as dict values (100 Days calculator) is B08 higher_order_functions. Reading word data from files into dicts is B10 file_io; json is B10.

sets.notes: Three core topics. Set comprehensions are dict_comprehensions.transform_dicts KP4. frozenset and the in-place operators (|=, &=) were left out (codecademy only). Big-O of set membership is a later algorithms batch.

nested_data_structures.notes: Grid topics own 2D lists; copying.shallow_vs_deep (B06, non-core) already teaches the [[0] * 3] * 3 trap and deepcopy, so it is not repeated; list_comprehensions.nested_comprehensions revisits safe grid building. match_structure_patterns adds the sequence patterns (B06 handoff) and mapping patterns (B04 handoff) in one non-core topic; it has no taught_in because none of the 8 courses teaches them. JSON parsing itself is B10 json_data, which should depend on navigate_deep_data. Recursion over nested lists/trees is B08 recursion.

list_comprehensions.notes: any()/all() and summing booleans (B05 handoff) are in any_all_and_sum. Its KP4 previews generator expressions only as 'brackets can go inside a call'; laziness, generator objects and yield are B08 generators, which should encompass any_all_and_sum. map()/filter() as alternatives are B08 higher_order_functions. Reconciliation: any_all_and_sum KP4 (dropping the brackets = generator expression preview) was removed; generators.generator_expressions (B08, the owner) now depends on any_all_and_sum.

dict_comprehensions.notes: Two topics; transform_dicts also owns set comprehensions.

stacks_queues.notes: Non-core (bootdev DSA and codecademy only). deque is taught here, so collections_module does not repeat it. Linked-list implementations are a later batch (linked_lists); recursion's call stack is B08.

collections_module.notes: Counter, defaultdict and namedtuple (B06 handoff); deque lives in stacks_queues.queue_with_deque. OrderedDict, ChainMap and UserDict/UserList were left out (plain dicts keep order since 3.7). 'from collections import X' is used as a memorised line before B13 modules_imports. dataclasses as the modern record type belong to the OOP batch (B11).

itertools_module.notes: Two non-core topics. zip(strict=True) (B06 handoff) is chain_count_zip_longest KP4. groupby, accumulate, islice and cycle were left out; generator pipelines are B08 generators.

higher_order_functions.notes: Functions as values, as arguments, as key functions (B06 left key=<own function> here) and map/filter. Returning functions is owned by closures.function_factories. Storing functions as dict values (100 Days calculator) was not written because dicts are B07 (parallel); a stitching pass may add a KP to functions_are_values or a B07 practice item. map/filter use lists and range only; map/filter vs comprehensions is B07's to compare. Reconciliation: functions stored in a dict (dispatch tables, 100 Days calculator) is now dispatch_tables.

lambda_functions.notes: key=lambda (deferred by B06 sorting) is lambda_as_argument KP1-2, which encompasses sorting.sort_tuples_and_keys. Sorting dict items with key=lambda kv: kv[1] belongs to B07 dictionaries and can encompass lambda_as_argument.

closures.notes: Owns enclosing scope, LEGB and nonlocal (deferred by B05 scope). The late-binding trap (lambdas made in a loop) is function_factories KP4. nonlocal_state is non-core: decorators do not depend on it.

currying.notes: One non-core topic (bootdev only). Includes functools.partial, imported with a single memorised from-import line, as B06 did with import copy, ahead of B13 modules_imports.

decorators.notes: General function decorators only. @property, @classmethod and @staticmethod belong to the OOP batch (B11), Flask @app.route to the web batch, @pytest.fixture to B09 lib_pytest, @contextmanager to B10 context_managers; all can build on decorators.at_syntax. Timing decorators need the time module (B13) and retry decorators need try/except (B09), so neither is used here. general_wrappers needs args_kwargs.unpack_in_calls.

generators.notes: All non-core, because they build on iteration.iter_and_next (non-core in B04). If iteration becomes core, yield_values and generator_expressions are good core candidates. generator_expressions has pending concept:list_comprehensions (B07, parallel); B05 asked B07 to cover any()/all() with generator expressions, so the stitching pass should check B07 did not also write a generator-expression topic (keep this one, have B07 encompass it or vice versa). send(), throw() and close() (codecademy only) were left out. Generators as context managers (@contextmanager) are B10. itertools is B07. Reconciliation: iteration.iter_and_next, yield_values and generator_expressions are core; lazy_and_infinite and pipelines stay non-core.

args_kwargs.notes: star_kwargs has pending concept:dictionaries (B07): kwargs is a dict, and only dict literal printing, d[key] and looping over keys are used. unpack_in_calls teaches f(*seq) from scratch so it can stay core, and encompasses B06 unpacking.star_unpacking (non-core) as non_ancestor. The keyword-only / positional-only markers (* and /) that B05 deferred are a non-core topic. Reconciliation: unpack_in_calls now depends on unpacking.star_unpacking (promoted to core) instead of re-teaching * in calls from scratch.

recursion.notes: Seven topics despite 4 courses because those teach it deep and it is a classic failure point. nested_lists is non-core with pending concept:nested_data_structures (B07) and uses type(x) == list, since isinstance is B11. Memoising with a hand-written dict is left to the stitching pass or a later algorithms batch (dicts are B07); memoize_with_cache uses functools.cache instead. Recursion on trees, binary search, merge sort and the static site generator belong to later data structures/algorithms batches and should depend on recursion_on_sequences and multiple_recursive_calls. Mathematical induction was not given a topic here. Reconciliation: nested_lists now uses isinstance(item, list) (objects_methods.isinstance_checks) and depends on nested_data_structures.grid_index_and_loop.

pure_functions.notes: One non-core topic (bootdev only); builds on B05 decomposition.one_job_per_function as B05 asked. B09 unit_testing could list it as a motivating prerequisite.

functional_programming.notes: Problem-based, non-core. Its parts (higher_order_functions, lambda_functions, closures, pure_functions) own their own topics. Comprehensions as the idiomatic alternative to map/filter are B07. Sum types (bootdev) need classes/enums and are left to B11.

debugging.notes: Full traceback reading (deferred by B01) is read_tracebacks; f"{x=}" (deferred by B03) is in print_debugging. The editor debugger (deferred by B01 ide_editor) is use_a_debugger, non-core because it needs an editor with a debugger. KeyError and FileNotFoundError are not in common_error_types: dicts (B07) and files (B10) run in parallel and should show their own errors. Hand-tracing with trace tables is practised inside systematic_process rather than given its own topic. Rubber-duck debugging and logging (the logging module) were not given topics.

exceptions.notes: try/except on bad input (deferred by B02/B04) starts in try_except_basics; the re-ask loop is defensive_programming.get_int_helper. try/except around open() and FileNotFoundError belong to B10 file_io, and finally-for-closing-files / with to B10 context_managers, which should encompass exceptions.else_and_finally. KeyError handling and dict.get as the alternative belong to B07 dictionaries. Exceptions in Selenium/Tkinter projects are left to those library batches. Exception hierarchy is touched only via LookupError in several_handlers_and_as KP4.

raising_exceptions.notes: Re-raising with a bare raise is exceptions.propagation KP4. custom_exceptions teaches 'class X(Exception): pass' as a template and has pending concept:classes; the OOP batch (inheritance) should encompass it and may add exception attributes / __init__. Raising in constructors (validating attributes) belongs to the OOP batch (constructors). raise ... from e (exception chaining) was not given a topic.

defensive_programming.notes: Concept is titled 'Input validation'. Range-only re-prompting is B04 while_loops.input_validation; this batch adds non-numeric input. Validating with regular expressions (cs50p Week 7) belongs to the regular_expressions batch, which should encompass clean_and_validate_text. Preconditions as specs are B05 docstrings.specifications; raising on bad arguments is raising_exceptions.raise_builtin.

assertions.notes: Only one topic: using assert to write tests is owned by unit_testing (test_function_with_asserts), since assertions 'is part of' unit_testing.

unit_testing.notes: Depends on functions.main_and_helpers as B05 suggested, not on main_guard (which waits for B13). Core topics keep tests in the same file as the code, so no import is needed; test files that import the code are lib_pytest (pending concept:modules_imports). Doctests (deferred by B05 docstrings) are unit_testing.doctests, non-core and taught by no course. unittest_module needs class syntax (pending concept:classes). Test fixtures, skipping, mocking and parametrised tests were not given topics (codecademy only); testing printed output (capsys) also left out.

lib_pytest.notes: Non-core: needs a terminal and an installed package. 'pip install pytest' is shown as a memorised line; installing packages is tool_pip / third_party_packages in a later batch, which could become a prerequisite. 'with pytest.raises' uses with before B10 context_managers, as a memorised form. @pytest.mark.parametrize needs decorators (B08) and was left out; a later stitching pass could add it. Reconciliation: write_and_run_tests now depends on modules_imports.own_modules and tool_pip.pip_install; raises_and_test_folders on modules_imports.packages_and_import_errors.

tool_mypy.notes: One non-core topic (cs50p introduces it only). Uses list[str] in one example; container hints are B06/B07. Strict mode and mypy configuration were left out.

file_io.notes: open_and_read teaches open/read/close once; every later topic uses with (context_managers.with_open, owned by context_managers but taught second). Loops over file lines (deferred by B03/B04) are file_io.loop_over_lines. handle_missing_file only applies try/except to files and has pending concept:exceptions (B09 owns try/except itself); if B09 writes its own FileNotFoundError example the stitching pass should make B09's generic try/except topic the prerequisite and keep this file-specific one. encoding='utf-8' (deferred by B03 unicode_encoding) is in encodings_and_binary. Binary images with PIL are B19 lib_pillow. Counting words in a file with a dict (py4e ch. 9) is B07 dictionaries, which can list file_io.loop_over_lines as a prerequisite in a later stitch. `import` lines (csv, json, os, sys) are used as memorised one-liners before B13 modules_imports, as B06 did with `import copy`.

context_managers.notes: with_open is the second file topic and core. write_with_contextlib is non-core (Codecademy only) and pending on concept:generators (yield, B08) and concept:exceptions (try/finally, B09); @contextmanager is used as a memorised line rather than requiring B08 decorators. Class-based context managers (__enter__/__exit__) belong to B11 dunder_methods. Nested managers are file_io.copy_and_transform KP2.

file_paths.notes: Non-core: the browser platform's files sit next to the program, so core file topics use bare names. Terminal-side paths are B01 command_line.absolute_and_relative_paths (a prerequisite). os.path string functions are owned here; filesystem changes (listdir, mkdir, rename, remove) are os_sys_module.

csv_files.notes: Manual split(';') parsing (Helsinki 'Reading CSV files') is file_io.parse_lines_into_data; csv.reader is motivated by its failure on quoted commas. dict_reader_writer has pending concept:dictionaries (B07). pandas read_csv is B18 lib_pandas. Sorting rows by a column needs key=lambda (B08) and was left to that batch's practice.

json_data.notes: json_strings KP1 uses lists only so it works before dicts; KP3-4 and later topics need dicts, hence pending concept:dictionaries. navigate_nested_json is pending concept:nested_data_structures (B07). JSON from HTTP APIs (requests .json()) is B16 apis_http, which should depend on navigate_nested_json. Handling a missing JSON file on first run combines json_data.json_files with file_io.handle_missing_file (practice item for later stitching, not a separate topic).

lib_json.notes: The json module (loads/dumps/load/dump, indent, JSONDecodeError) is fully taught by the json_data topics; a separate topic would duplicate them.

serialization.notes: Only Boot.dev teaches it (in Go, for pub/sub, which is out of scope). One non-core topic that generalises JSON/CSV/text and introduces pickle. Serializing custom objects (to_dict/from_dict) belongs to B11 classes.

os_sys_module.notes: sys.argv is owned by command_line_args; os.path string functions by file_paths; os.environ by B13 environment_variables; subprocess by B13. shutil (copying/removing folder trees) was left out. Uses `import os` / `import sys` before B13 modules_imports as memorised lines.

command_line_args.notes: Non-core because running with arguments needs a terminal (B01 running_scripts.run_from_terminal is non-core); a browser platform would need an 'arguments' box to make these core. *args/**kwargs (which the concept graph places after this) are B08. Validating with try/except int() is B09 practice.

cli_applications.notes: Project-shaped (Boot.dev BookBot, Pokedex REPL): best delivered as multisteps; these two topics teach the reusable structure. Character counting with dicts and sorting the report (BookBot) need B07 dictionaries and B08 key functions and are left as later practice. Command dispatch through a dict of functions is B08 higher_order_functions.

objects_methods.notes: types_and_methods is the bridge from built-in methods to self (obj.method(x) == Class.method(obj, x)). isinstance (B02/B05 handoff) is isinstance_checks; isinstance with subclasses is B12 inheritance, which should encompass it. B08 recursion.nested_lists used type(x) == list and can now switch to isinstance in a stitch. object_references owns aliasing of user-defined objects (B06 handoff); objects as attributes of other objects ('has-a', Helsinki Part 9) is B12 composition. Canvas object methods (Code in Place) belong to the graphics batch.

classes.notes: Seven topics: define_and_instantiate, then (after instance_attributes.set_and_read and constructors.init_sets_attributes) the method topics, collections of objects, records_as_classes (data abstraction, B05 handoff, plus to_dict for B10's serialisation handoff) and dataclasses (B07 handoff). CapWords naming (B01 handoff) is define_and_instantiate KP3. dataclasses is non-core with no taught_in (none of the 8 courses teaches it) but is the modern record type; B12 sum_types may want it as a prerequisite, which would justify promoting it to core. Class patterns in match (B04 handoff, case Point(x=0)) were NOT written here: they fit B12 sum_types, which runs in parallel; if B12 did not write them, a stitch should add a KP to classes.dataclasses or enums.enums_in_logic. Project-shaped class work (Quiz Game, Coffee Machine, Asteroids) is multistep material. unittest_module (B09, pending concept:classes) can now depend on classes.define_methods.

instance_attributes.notes: set_and_read comes before __init__ (Helsinki/py4e order) and motivates it with the silent-typo bug. getattr/setattr/hasattr/vars (codecademy 'Attribute Functions') are a non-core topic. __slots__ was left out.

constructors.notes: init_sets_attributes, defaults_and_derived (includes the mutable default in __init__, encompassing B05 parameters_arguments.mutable_default_trap as non_ancestor because that topic is non-core) and validate_in_init (B09 handoff: raising in constructors). __del__/object lifecycle (py4e) was left out. Custom exception classes with their own __init__ and super().__init__ need inheritance and belong to B12, which should encompass raising_exceptions.custom_exceptions (B09 asked for this). Reconciliation: defaults_and_derived now depends on parameters_arguments.mutable_default_trap (promoted to core) instead of a non_ancestor encompassing.

class_attributes.notes: Owns @classmethod and @staticmethod (B08 handoff). classmethods also owns from_dict, the partner of classes.records_as_classes' to_dict (B10 serialisation handoff). @classmethod is taught as a marker line; decorators.at_syntax is not a prerequisite here (it is for encapsulation.read_only_properties). Why cls instead of the class name (subclasses) is for B12 inheritance. staticmethods is non-core (cs50p only).

encapsulation.notes: private_by_convention (_x, __x name mangling, getter/setter methods), read_only_properties and property_setters (@property, B08 handoff, built on decorators.at_syntax). The OOP 'abstraction' pillar as interface vs implementation is classes.records_as_classes KP3; abstract base classes are B12 abstract_classes.

dunder_methods.notes: Six topics: str_and_repr, equality_and_ordering and operator_overloading are core; container_methods, custom_iterators (B04 iteration handoff) and context_manager_protocol (B10 handoff: __enter__/__exit__) are non-core. __hash__ (an object with __eq__ becomes unhashable) was not given a KP because sets/dicts are not ancestors of equality_and_ordering; classes.dataclasses KP4 mentions that frozen dataclasses are hashable. functools.total_ordering, __call__, __bool__ (only the __len__ fallback is taught), __iadd__ and __radd__/sum() were left out. Overriding dunder methods as polymorphism is B12.

enums.notes: Two non-core topics (bootdev only). define_and_use and enums_in_logic (match on members, the B04 match handoff for value patterns; auto() and StrEnum). Named constants for magic numbers stay with B02 constants; enums_in_logic encompasses nothing from it. Sum types built from enums or dataclasses are B12 sum_types, which should list enums.define_and_use as a prerequisite. Flag and IntEnum were left out. 'from enum import Enum' is a memorised line before B13 modules_imports.

inheritance.notes: Class basics (class, __init__, self, attributes, methods) are B11 and enter via pending concept:classes / concept:constructors on define_subclass; encapsulation (_ and __ conventions) is B11, so multilevel_hierarchies only adds what happens to __private names in subclasses (Helsinki 'access modifiers') and has pending concept:encapsulation. isinstance is introduced here only as the is-a check (define_subclass KP4); if B11 teaches isinstance on its own, the stitching pass should make that a prerequisite. exception_hierarchies takes the B09 handoff (custom exceptions with __init__/attributes, catching a family, handler order) and encompasses raising_exceptions.custom_exceptions. multiple_inheritance (MRO, mixins, diamond super) is non-core, codecademy only. Overriding __str__/__eq__ and other dunders is B11 dunder_methods. Reconciliation: pending concept:classes/constructors resolved to classes.define_methods; isinstance now comes from objects_methods.isinstance_checks (prerequisite of define_subclass); multilevel_hierarchies depends on encapsulation.private_by_convention.

polymorphism.notes: Operator overloading (__add__, __len__, __eq__) is B11 dunder_methods; polymorphism.same_call_different_classes KP4 only shows that built-ins already behave polymorphically. parent_calls_overridden_method is the template-method idea and is the hinge for abstract_classes. Duck typing comes last because it generalises overriding to unrelated classes.

composition.notes: Only Helsinki teaches it ('objects as attributes'), but it is a core design tool, so three core topics. Aliasing of contained objects takes the B06 handoff ('aliasing of objects/attributes is the OOP batch'). has_a_vs_is_a also serves as the 'composition over inheritance' part of object_oriented_design. Linked lists and trees (objects holding objects of the same class) are B15.

abstract_classes.notes: One non-core topic (codecademy introduces it). Uses 'from abc import ABC, abstractmethod' and @abstractmethod as memorised lines, as earlier batches did with imports and decorators. Abstract properties and abstract class methods were left out.

interfaces.notes: Only Boot.dev teaches interfaces, in Go. Python's equivalents are duck-typed interfaces, ABCs and typing.Protocol; both topics are non-core. typing_protocol has empty taught_in (none of the courses teaches Protocol) and depends on tool_mypy (non-core, needs a terminal). The fake-object-for-tests idea is a KP here; mocking libraries were not given a topic. Generics (which 'interfaces comes before') are out of scope.

sum_types.notes: Boot.dev's Functional Programming 'Sum Types' chapter. Variants are plain classes because dataclasses belong to B11 (running in parallel); if B11 teaches dataclasses, the stitching pass may rewrite these examples with @dataclass (and then positional class patterns like Circle(r) work). match class patterns (deferred by B04) live in match_class_patterns, which uses keyword patterns so plain classes work. Union aliases use Shape = Circle | Rect rather than the 3.12 'type' statement. Pending concept:enums for the enum-vs-sum-type KP and concept:classes (which should provide isinstance, per the B02 note).

object_oriented_design.notes: Meta-skill taught as three problem-based core topics (identify classes, refactor procedural code into a class, design collaborating objects). Class basics are B11; the four pillars are owned by their concepts (encapsulation B11, inheritance/polymorphism/abstract classes here). Larger OOP projects (Coffee Machine, Quiz, Turtle Crossing, Helsinki's larger application) are project-shaped and best delivered as multisteps built on these topics. SOLID principles and UML class diagrams were not given topics.

clean_code.notes: Boot.dev's OOP 'Clean Code' chapter. Two non-core problem-based topics; naming and one-job functions are already B05 (decomposition.one_job_per_function), named constants B02 and guard clauses B04 (flatten_nesting), so spot_code_smells links and encompasses those rather than re-teaching them. Linters/formatters are B01 pep8_style.linters_and_formatters. Class naming (CapWords) belongs with B11 classes.

modules_imports.notes: Owns import X / from X import Y / as / own modules / packages. Earlier batches used memorised one-line imports (import copy B06; from collections/itertools/functools B07-B08; import csv/json/os/sys/argparse/pickle, from pathlib/contextlib B10; import unittest/pytest B09): import_module KP3 and from_import_and_alias KP2 practise reading and rewriting exactly those lines, with small non_ancestor encompassings of copying.shallow_vs_deep, json_data.json_strings and collections_module.counter. Stitching: main_guard.if_name_main's pending concept:modules_imports resolves to modules_imports.own_modules (KP3 'importing runs top-level code' sets up the guard); lib_pytest.write_and_run_tests' pending resolves to modules_imports.own_modules, and lib_pytest.raises_and_test_folders (tests/ folder, __init__.py) should list modules_imports.packages_and_import_errors. Module-level globals across files (B05 scope handoff) appear only in own_modules KP1-2; a module's own global namespace was not given a separate KP. Relative imports, importlib, __all__ and the time module (B08 wanted time.perf_counter for timing decorators) were left out.

random_module.notes: Guessing game with a random secret (B04 handoff) is random_games KP1; random.choice on lists (B06 handoff) is choice_shuffle_sample. Estimating probabilities by repeated simulation is B14 simulation_monte_carlo, which should depend on random_numbers and choice_shuffle_sample; random colours for graphics are B19. Examples avoid comprehensions and print only values that do not depend on the random draw.

math_module.notes: math.pi (B02 constants handoff) and math.isclose (B02 comparison_operators handoff) are here. B14 floating_point_precision (parallel) owns binary representation, epsilon reasoning and decimal; if it also teaches isclose, keep isclose_and_inf KP1-2 and have B14 encompass it. Trig functions and radians were left out (only needed by graphics/games batches).

datetime_module.notes: Date format specs in f-strings (B03 handoff) are format_and_parse KP2. Time zones, the time module (time.sleep, time.time) and calendar were left out; scheduling (B16 scheduling_cron) and pandas datetime conversion (B18) build on these topics.

statistics_module.notes: One non-core topic (cs50p introduces it only). Hypothesis testing and numpy/pandas statistics are B18.

tool_pip.notes: All non-core (needs a terminal). pip/venv deferred by B01 python_setup. B09 lib_pytest used 'pip install pytest' as a memorised line; a stitching pass could add tool_pip.pip_install as its prerequisite. pipenv/poetry/uv were not given topics: they automate the same venv + requirements workflow.

third_party_packages.notes: General skills only; each named library (requests, pygame, pillow, cowsay, ...) is owned by its lib_ concept in B16-B19, which should depend on find_and_install. learn_from_docs uses PrettyTable (100 Days Day 16), which no lib_ concept owns; its snippets were not run (not installed), so its output is described rather than quoted. Attribute assignment on an object (table.field_names = ...) is used as copied-from-docs before B11 classes.

regular_expressions.notes: Regex validation (B09 handoff) is anchors_and_validation, which depends on and encompasses defensive_programming.clean_and_validate_text. Raw strings come from B03 strings.multiline_and_raw. Named groups, lookarounds, re.compile and verbose mode were left out; HTML parsing with regex vs BeautifulSoup belongs to B16 web_scraping, Markdown parsing to B20.

environment_variables.notes: os.environ (B10 os_sys_module handoff) is read_environment. Both non-core (terminal). The concept graph puts this after apis_http (B16, later wave); examples use a placeholder WEATHER_API_KEY without making HTTP calls, so B16 apis_http can depend on secrets_out_of_code. Deployment config (B17) builds on it. The python-dotenv snippet was not run (package not installed).

subprocess_module.notes: One non-core topic (bootdev AI agent runs Python files with a timeout). The agent's sandboxing and function-calling are B20. Popen, pipes between processes and shell=True usage were left out on purpose.

tool_jupyter.notes: One non-core topic; pandas inside notebooks is B18. Magics beyond %pip and notebook display of DataFrames/plots were left to B18.

guess_and_check.notes: Owns exhaustive enumeration and the stepping/epsilon approximation (MIT L4-L5), as B04 loop_patterns and B05 computational_thinking deferred. Bisection and Newton build on approximate_with_epsilon.

bisection_method.notes: Two topics (MIT only, deep). Bisection on numbers; bisection on list positions is binary_search, which depends on bisection_square_root. The integer guessing game appears only as a practice item; with random secrets it needs B13 random_module.

newton_raphson.notes: One non-core topic; derivatives are given as formulas, not taught.

floating_point_precision.notes: B02 integers_floats / comparison_operators already teach 0.1 + 0.2, round() and abs(a - b) < tol; these topics are not repeated. math.isclose is left to B13 math_module (sibling), which could encompass accumulating_errors. Decimal/Fraction (codecademy) imports are memorised one-liners for B13 to link back to. Reconciliation: math.isclose stays with B13 math_module.isclose_and_inf (no duplicate here); decimal_and_fraction now depends on and encompasses it.

binary_bitwise.notes: read_binary and the % 2 / // 2 conversion loop (MIT L4); bitwise operators (Boot.dev 'Computing'). All non-core: nothing later in the plan is expected to depend on them. B02 deferred ^ here.

linear_search.notes: One core topic; list.index/in as built-in linear search is mentioned, not re-taught (B06 owns them).

binary_search.notes: Iterative version is core; bugs and recursive/bisect versions are non-core. Recursive version with slicing vs indexes ties to complexity_big_o.cost_of_builtin_operations. import bisect is a memorised one-liner for B13.

sorting_algorithms.notes: Bubble, selection, merge (MIT L24) and insertion, quick (Boot.dev) plus a comparison topic containing bogo sort and stability. sorted()/sort()/key= are B06 sorting and B08; not re-taught. Bogo sort uses import random as a memorised one-liner (random.shuffle).

complexity_big_o.notes: Timing, counting, Big O/Theta, classes and built-in operation costs (MIT L21-L23, L26 'lists in memory, hashing'). Big O of set/dict membership (deferred by B07) is cost_of_builtin_operations KP1; hash table internals are B15 hash_maps_internals, which should depend on cost_of_builtin_operations. timing_programs uses import time as a memorised one-liner (B13 has no time-module concept).

simulation_monte_carlo.notes: Both topics need random.randint/random.random/random.seed, owned by B13 random_module (sibling), hence pending concept:random_module; the snippets use import random as a memorised line. Random walks and full games (Code in Place 'Simulations and games') are left as multistep projects.

mathematical_induction.notes: One non-core topic placed after B08 recursion.base_and_recursive_case (B08 left it without a topic); the concept graph puts induction before recursion, but the topic uses recursive functions as its main application.

linked_lists.notes: Node and LinkedList classes are used before B11 teaches classes: entry topics carry pending concept:classes and present the class lines as a copied template. Making the list iterable with __iter__/yield and __repr__ (Boot.dev) was left to B11 dunder_methods. Step-count comparisons carry pending concept:complexity_big_o (B14). Doubly linked lists were not given a topic. Reconciliation: Node/LinkedList are now taught classes (pending concept:classes resolved to constructors.init_sets_attributes); long examples trimmed to the changed lines. reverse_in_place kept: a distinct, classic pointer exercise with no overlap.

trees.notes: Builds on B08 recursion (multiple_recursive_calls, recursion_on_sequences) as B08's note asked. BST search carries pending concept:binary_search (B14) because it is the tree form of the same idea. Level-order traversal is graph_algorithms.breadth_first_search. Duplicate values in a BST go right and are not discussed further. general_trees uses isinstance as a copied line before B11/B12.

balanced_trees.notes: Red-black only (Boot.dev). Insert fix-up is traced, not implemented with parent pointers; rotations are written without parent pointers. Red-black deletion and AVL trees were left out.

tries.notes: Nested dicts with a '*' end marker, as in Boot.dev; plain functions instead of a Trie class, so no classes dependency.

graphs.notes: Graphs are dicts of sets/dicts and lists of lists, so no classes dependency. Examples iterate sorted(graph[v]) because set order of strings varies between runs.

graph_algorithms.notes: BFS/DFS/paths from Boot.dev; pagerank_iteration from py4e (introduced only). Weighted shortest paths (Dijkstra), topological sort and cycle detection in directed graphs are taught by none of the 8 courses and were left out. Uses `from collections import deque` (B07). Grid KPs build neighbour lists with plain loops.

hash_maps_internals.notes: Plain functions over a bucket list instead of Boot.dev's HashMap class, so no classes dependency. __hash__/__eq__ for user classes belongs to B11 dunder_methods. Average-case O(1) reasoning carries pending concept:complexity_big_o.

p_vs_np.notes: One topic: Boot.dev only, introduced. Exponential running time itself belongs to B14 complexity_big_o (pending).

apis_http.notes: HTTP/API concepts only; the requests library is lib_requests and urllib is lib_urllib. Worked examples with live endpoints use canned JSON (as Python data) and say what the live call returns. Rate limits (429) are lib_requests.handle_errors and automation.reliable_bots. Building your own API (REST design, Flask routes) is B17 rest_api_design, which should list apis_http.request_response_cycle (methods, status codes) as a prerequisite. OAuth flows (Spotipy) and SMS (Twilio) were not given topics: library-specific and project-shaped. LLM APIs (B20) can depend on lib_requests.send_data_and_headers. Every B16 topic is non-core: none run in a browser sandbox without network access.

lib_requests.notes: Snippets were checked offline with requests 2.31 under the system Python 3.9 (requests.Request(...).prepare() for URLs and bodies, hand-built Response objects for .json() and raise_for_status); no live calls. Sessions, file uploads and streaming downloads were left out.

lib_urllib.notes: urllib.request (py4e's urlopen) plus urllib.parse; urllib.robotparser is used in web_scraping.scrape_responsibly. urlopen behaviour was checked offline with data: URLs.

web_scraping.notes: html_css_basics is out of scope (plan.json), so html_and_regex KP1 teaches just enough HTML (tags, attributes, nesting, class/id) to scrape. follow_links stands in a dict of link lists for fetch+parse so the crawl logic is testable; it encompasses graph_algorithms.breadth_first_search as non_ancestor. Ethics of scraping (100 Days Day 45) is scrape_responsibly. Teaching order: html_and_regex, scrape_responsibly, then lib_beautifulsoup topics, then scrape_to_records and follow_links.

lib_beautifulsoup.notes: bs4 is not installed here, so these snippets were NOT run; outputs follow documented Beautiful Soup 4 behaviour (find returns None, get vs [] on attributes, get_text(strip=True), select/select_one). Navigating siblings/parents and lxml as a parser were left out.

lib_selenium.notes: Not installed and needs a browser, so snippets were not run; written against the Selenium 4 API (By locators, find_element/find_elements; the old find_element_by_* methods are gone). Login automation for real social sites (100 Days Days 49-52) is project-shaped and was not given topics; the form-filling KP uses a generic form.

xml_parsing.notes: xml_documents (format) comes before the lib_elementtree topics; read_rss_feed (Boot.dev's RSS aggregator, py4e XML) comes after them. Using defusedxml for untrusted XML and XML Schema (py4e lecture) were not given KPs. Writing XML was left out.

lib_elementtree.notes: Uses 'import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET' (B13 from_import_and_alias covers the alias form). Creating and writing XML (SubElement, ET.tostring) was left out: no course teaches it.

web_services.notes: One non-core topic (py4e lecture, introduced). Includes the fetch/parse split so parsers can be tested with canned text. SOAP/WSDL were not taught.

networking_sockets.notes: One conceptual topic placed before apis_http, as the concept graph says. DNS, TLS and HTTP servers are out of scope per plan.json; TLS appears only as starttls in lib_smtplib.

lib_socket.notes: py4e's socket browser. send/recv behaviour was checked locally with socket.socketpair() (no network). Writing a socket server was left out (http_servers is out of scope).

tool_geocoding_api.notes: Uses py4e's current OpenGeo endpoint and its GeoJSON reply shape (features[0].properties.lat/lon/formatted); replies are canned. py4e's geoload.py caches in SQLite; here the cache is a dict/JSON file because sqlite3 is B17 (sibling). B17 lib_sqlite3 could add a practice item that swaps the cache for a table. Drawing the map itself is B18 data_visualization.

lib_smtplib.notes: smtplib calls need a real server and credentials, so only message building (string format, EmailMessage, encode errors) was run. Contact-form email from Flask (100 Days Day 60) belongs to B17 lib_flask and can depend on email_messages_and_templates. Attachments and HTML email were left out.

automation.notes: Problem-based topics built on the 100 Days birthday wisher, price tracker and rain alert. Concrete tools are owned by lib_smtplib, lib_selenium, lib_pyautogui and scheduling_cron. Logging uses plain file appends; the logging module has no concept in the plan. time.sleep is used as a memorised 'import time' line (B13 has no time-module concept). Bots that log in to real social sites were not given topics.

lib_pyautogui.notes: One non-core topic (100 Days Day 94, introduced). Not installed and needs a desktop, so snippets were not run. Screenshot-based image location (locateOnScreen) was left out.

scheduling_cron.notes: 100 Days Day 32 (PythonAnywhere). The third-party 'schedule' package and GitHub Actions cron were not given topics. B17 deployment can build on cron_and_cloud_schedulers.

databases_sql.notes: SQL is taught as its own language, run through sqlite3 in-memory databases (all snippets executed). Entry topic uses `import sqlite3` / `connect(':memory:')` / `execute` as a three-line template that lib_sqlite3.connect_execute_fetch explains immediately after. INTEGER PRIMARY KEY mechanics live in constraints; choosing keys and foreign keys belong to data_modeling. Indexes (CREATE INDEX), normalization theory, PostgreSQL, DB Browser for SQLite and migrations are out of scope per plan.json; a logical key's UNIQUE constraint is the only performance idea taught. CASE expressions, views, transactions beyond commit/rollback, window functions and UPSERT (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE) were left out. manage_tables and subqueries are non-core.

lib_sqlite3.notes: Owns the Python side: connect/execute/fetch, placeholders and SQL injection (the injection_attacks concept is out of scope, so its sqlite3-relevant part lives here), commit/with/executescript, lastrowid/rowcount/IntegrityError, sqlite3.Row, and a file-loading topic (py4e counting-email pattern). Uses `import csv`/`import json` as earlier batches did. B18 pandas.read_sql could depend on connect_execute_fetch.

sql_joins.notes: inner_join is core; left_join and multi_table_joins are non-core. Self-joins, RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN (FULL needs SQLite 3.39+) and CROSS JOIN by name were left out; the every-combination bug covers the cross-join idea.

data_modeling.notes: py4e Chapter 15 data modeling: split_into_tables (a practical 'normalization' without normal forms), keys, get_or_create_id (py4e Tracks pattern) and many_to_many. ER diagram notation is described in text (artists 1 --< albums) rather than given a topic.

lib_sqlalchemy.notes: SQLAlchemy 2.0 declarative style (DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, select, Session) rather than the legacy Query API; Flask-SQLAlchemy (100 Days' actual tool) is its own topic. Not installed locally, so snippets were not run; outputs (echo SQL, ids) are described from the documented behaviour. Alembic migrations are out of scope (db_migrations).

web_development.notes: Server-side view only. how_web_apps_work models routing as a dict of functions (runnable without Flask) and introduces 200/404/500 from the server's side; the client side of HTTP (methods, headers, status codes, requests library) is B16 apis_http, running in parallel, and the stitching pass should link B16's request/response topic as a prerequisite of how_web_apps_work or have it encompass that KP. html_css_basics is out of scope, but Flask needs a little HTML, so html_for_python_devs teaches tags, links, forms and html.escape (XSS) only; CSS and Bootstrap are not taught. Static site generation is B20. Reconciliation: how_web_apps_work now depends on B16 apis_http.request_response_cycle (owner of HTTP requests, responses, methods and status codes); KP1 and KP3 were reframed as the server side instead of re-teaching them.

lib_flask.notes: Five non-core topics following 100 Days Days 54-62. Flask is not installed, so no snippet was run; Flask's test_client is taught in KP3 of first_app_and_routes so the platform can auto-grade views without a browser. Blueprints, the application factory, Flask's g and before_request were left out (no course teaches them). Sessions/login live in authentication; JSON APIs in rest_api_design; database access in lib_sqlalchemy.flask_sqlalchemy.

lib_jinja.notes: Three non-core topics. Only expressions_and_filters KP1 uses jinja2.Template directly; the rest are Flask templates. Macros, custom filters and whitespace control were left out.

lib_wtforms.notes: Flask-WTF + WTForms (100 Days Days 61-62). Bootstrap-Flask's render_form (Flask-Bootstrap) is lib_bootstrap, out of scope. Not installed; error texts quoted from WTForms' standard messages.

authentication.notes: Six non-core topics. Hashing, salting and pbkdf2 use hashlib/secrets from the standard library and were run; register_and_login was run end to end with sqlite3. werkzeug, Flask-Login and JWT are described, not run. Authorization (out of scope as its own concept) appears only as the admin_only decorator KP in login_sessions. api_tokens comes after rest_api_design.write_endpoints. MFA/TOTP, OAuth sign-in and password reset flows were left out.

rest_api_design.notes: Three non-core topics (100 Days Day 66). resources_and_methods carries pending concept:apis_http (B16) because it reuses HTTP methods and status codes from the client view; it re-states them only as a design table. Endpoints use sqlite3 + sqlite3.Row rather than SQLAlchemy so they need only core database topics plus Flask; the SQLAlchemy version is a practice variation. Pagination, versioning and OpenAPI were left out; API keys in DELETE are the bridge to authentication.api_tokens.

deployment.notes: Two non-core topics (100 Days Day 71). Git/GitHub, Docker, PostgreSQL administration and HTTPS are out of scope; pushing to GitHub appears as a memorised step. Builds on B13 environment_variables.secrets_out_of_code and tool_pip.requirements_files as B13 suggested.

data_analysis.notes: Umbrella-like process concept: the library skills live in lib_pandas; these two problem-based topics teach the workflow and sanity checks. Text analysis (Boot.dev BookBot) is covered by B07 dictionaries.counting_pattern and B10 cli_applications; py4e's spider/visualise pipelines by B16/B17. Portfolio projects (Days 99-100) are multistep material built from these topics.

lib_numpy.notes: Five topics (Day 77): arrays, vectorised ops, indexing, boolean masks, axes/broadcasting/@. Installing numpy (pip/%pip) is third_party_packages.find_and_install and is not a prerequisite: the browser platform is assumed to ship numpy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, plotly, scipy and scikit-learn. Images as 3D arrays (Day 77 image manipulation, Day 92 colour palette) are left to B19 image_processing, which can depend on lib_numpy.index_and_slice. np.random.default_rng is used once (statistics_hypothesis_testing.distributions_and_spread) as a recipe line. Snippets were run with NumPy 2.0.2.

lib_pandas.notes: Ten topics (100 Days Days 25-26, 31-32, 72-76). Entry depends on lib_numpy.vectorised_arithmetic so vectorisation and masks are taught once, in NumPy; 100 Days teaches pandas first, so a reviewer may prefer to cut that link. Examples print .tolist() and scalars rather than whole tables, because NumPy 2 scalar reprs (np.int64(12)) and table layout vary by version. pandas was not installed: these snippets were not run; outputs were checked by hand and by recomputing with NumPy. Reading a table from SQL (pd.read_sql) belongs to B17 databases_sql; pd.read_html scraping to B16 web_scraping; Tkinter flash cards (Day 31) use to_python_and_files and belong to B19.

data_visualization.notes: Library-independent chart choice and honesty; the drawing calls are owned by lib_matplotlib, lib_seaborn and lib_plotly. tool_d3js (py4e) is not in this batch's concept list and was not given a topic. Plot topics are graded by matching calls to chart sketches, predicting heights/counts, and fix-the-bug on arguments, since rendered images cannot be compared.

lib_matplotlib.notes: Entry topic needs only lists (MIT L25 plots lists), so it can be taught before pandas. Locators/date formatters (Day 75) were folded into plot_pandas_data practice rather than given a KP. Snippets were not run (matplotlib not installed); the quoted ValueError and TypeError texts are matplotlib's standard messages.

lib_seaborn.notes: Not run (seaborn not installed). regplot leads into linear_regression, but linear_regression does not depend on seaborn: numpy polyfit + matplotlib scatter carry the same idea.

lib_plotly.notes: plotly.express only (Days 76, 79); graph_objects was left out. Not run (plotly not installed).

lib_scipy.notes: One topic on calling scipy.stats; the meaning of tests is owned by statistics_hypothesis_testing. Not run (scipy not installed): the t statistic, p-values and r were recomputed independently with NumPy and numerical integration of the t distribution.

lib_scikit_learn.notes: One topic on the estimator API (fit/predict, 2D X, trailing-underscore attributes, train_test_split). Regression meaning is linear_regression. Not run (scikit-learn not installed); coefficients and R-squared were recomputed with numpy.polyfit/lstsq.

linear_regression.notes: Days 78 and 81. Feature scaling, regularisation and multicollinearity were left out (not taught by any course).

statistics_hypothesis_testing.notes: Day 80 (Semmelweis). p-values are introduced by a shuffling simulation in plain Python (run with 3.13) before scipy, building on B14 simulation_monte_carlo, so the t-test is not a black box. Confidence intervals, chi-squared and one-sided tests were left out.

graphics_canvas.notes: Library-independent graphics skills (coordinates, bounding boxes, loops of shapes, colours, animation and wall bouncing), all checkable as plain arithmetic so they run on any platform. Library APIs live in lib_stanford_graphics, lib_turtle, lib_tkinter and lib_pygame. Colours own RGB/hex conversion (B13 deferred random colours here). Collisions between objects are collision_detection.

lib_turtle.notes: 100 Days of Code Days 18-23. turtle is in the standard library (no pip). Turtle snippets were not run on screen; positions and headings were checked with turtle.TNavigator (the turtle's movement maths without a window), which also lets a platform grade 'predict the final position' items headlessly. Collisions in turtle games (distance() < n, wall and paddle checks) are collision_detection; scoreboards and game state are game_development. Snake-body and anti-reverse KPs run as plain lists.

lib_stanford_graphics.notes: Code in Place's graphics.Canvas (a browser-side library). Snippets were not run here (library not installable); method names follow the Code in Place handout (create_rectangle/oval/line/text, move, moveto, get_left_x, get_top_y, get_canvas_width, get_last_click). Point-in-rectangle hit tests for clicks are collision_detection.rectangles_and_responses.

lib_tkinter.notes: 100 Days of Code Days 27-31. tkinter is standard library but opens a window, so snippets were not run (only the mm:ss formatting KP was). The *args/**kwargs material of Day 27 is B08 args_kwargs. Data persistence in the Password Manager / Flash Card apps (json, pandas) is B10/B18. Images on a Tk Canvas (PhotoImage) were left out; Pillow images are lib_pillow.

event_driven_programming.notes: Library-independent and fully runnable: events are simulated with dicts of handlers and a list as the event queue. The library bindings (turtle onkey/onclick, tkinter command=/bind/after, pygame.event.get) are taught in lib_turtle, lib_tkinter and lib_pygame, which depend on these topics. Web request handlers (Flask routes, B16/B17) are the same idea and could encompass callbacks_and_registration in a stitch.

game_development.notes: Project-shaped: Snake, Pong, Turtle Crossing, Breakout, Space Invaders, Asteroids and Helsinki's own game are best delivered as multisteps built on these topics plus game_loop, collision_detection and a library (lib_turtle or lib_pygame). These four topics teach the reusable pieces in plain Python so they can be graded headlessly. Text games with random (guessing games) are B13 random_module.random_games.

lib_pygame.notes: Helsinki Part 13-14 and Boot.dev Asteroids. pygame was not installed, so snippets were not run; API names follow the pygame 2 docs. The library-independent ideas (game loop, dt, vectors, collisions) live in game_loop and collision_detection, so these topics only add the pygame calls. Sound, fonts (pygame.font) and Rect methods beyond colliderect were left out.

game_loop.notes: Library-independent; loops are simulated with lists of events and dt values so they run headlessly. pygame's Clock and event queue are taught in lib_pygame, which game_loop does not require. Turtle's tracer/update version is lib_turtle.smooth_animation_and_snake.

collision_detection.notes: Pure maths, runnable without a library. Trig (sin, cos, radians), which B13 math_module left to the games batch, is vectors_and_movement KP4. Wall bouncing is graphics_canvas.animation_loop; snake self-collision is lib_turtle.smooth_animation_and_snake KP4.

lib_pillow.notes: CS50P Week 6 (P-Shirt), MIT PS5 and 100 Days image projects. Pillow was not installed, so API snippets were not run; arithmetic KPs were. Pixel arithmetic itself is image_processing (runnable on nested lists). The B10 handoff (binary images with PIL) is open_resize_save, which lists file_io.encodings_and_binary as a prerequisite.

image_processing.notes: Pixel arithmetic on nested lists, independent of Pillow so it runs and grades headlessly; lib_pillow.pixel_data connects it to real image files. NumPy image arrays (100 Days Day 77) are B18 lib_numpy.

lib_cowsay.notes: Introduced only, as CS50P's first pip-install demo; one KP (KP1) in the shared fun-output topic. Installing packages is B13 third_party_packages.

lib_emoji.notes: One KP (KP2) in the shared fun-output topic (CS50P 'Emojize').

lib_pyfiglet.notes: One shared topic for the three CS50P 'fun output' libraries (cowsay, emoji, pyfiglet), one KP each plus the argv font-choice KP; owned here because pyfiglet carries the most skill. None was installed, so output was described from the docs, not run.

lib_inflect.notes: CS50P 'Adieu, Adieu' and 'Seasons of Love'. Not installed; outputs follow the inflect docs.

lib_tabulate.notes: CS50P 'Pizza Py'. Not installed; the sample table follows tabulate's documented 'simple' format. PrettyTable (100 Days) is B13 third_party_packages.learn_from_docs.

lib_fpdf.notes: CS50P 'CS50 Shirtificate'. Uses fpdf2's current cell(text=...) spelling (older versions used txt=). Not installed; only the centring arithmetic was run.

lib_validators.notes: CS50P 'Response Validation' (validators or validator-collection). Regex validation itself is B13 regular_expressions.anchors_and_validation, which this topic depends on. validator-collection's raising style (validators.email raises on failure; checkers.is_email returns bool) was not given a KP.

llm_apis.notes: Vendor-neutral: requests, responses, tool calls and agents are shown as plain dicts/JSON in the OpenAI chat-completions shape (which OpenRouter and many local servers share); no network calls, every response is a canned JSON string or dict parsed locally. Sending the request over HTTP is not taught here: B16 apis_http/lib_requests (sibling) owns the HTTP client side; a stitch could add apis_http as an optional prerequisite of chat_request_messages KP4 or of lib_openai.client_and_chat_completion. API keys come from B13 environment_variables.secrets_out_of_code. context_window_budget has empty taught_in (added: tokens/cost/history trimming are what Boot.dev's verbose token printing hints at). Streaming, embeddings/RAG and image inputs were left out (no course teaches them).

lib_openai.notes: Two non-core topics. SDK snippets were NOT run (openai is not installed and no network calls were allowed); they are described, and everything after the SDK boundary works on response.model_dump() dicts so it is tested with fakes. Boot.dev's current AI Agent uses the OpenAI SDK against OpenRouter (base_url), earlier versions Google Gemini. pip install is a memorised line; third_party_packages.find_and_install is the prerequisite.

function_calling.notes: Owns tool schemas, reading tool_calls (arguments as a JSON string), dispatch via a dict of functions with ** (closes the reconcile GAP 'functions stored in a dict / dispatch table' for this domain) and the role 'tool' result messages. Anthropic-style tool_use/tool_result blocks differ only in key names; not shown separately.

ai_agents.notes: Boot.dev's toy coding agent: agent_loop (scripted fake models), sandboxed_file_tools (get_files_info/get_file_content/write_file guard), run_code_tool (run_python_file via subprocess; takes the B13 subprocess_module handoff), observe_and_test_agent (verbose flag, token totals, tests). human_approval_and_safety (approval prompts, prompt injection, limits) is not taught by any course (empty taught_in) but is essential for real agents. Multi-agent systems, memory stores and agent frameworks were left out.

markdown.notes: Follows Boot.dev's SSG: TextNode/TextType (dataclass + enum, so it needs B11 classes.dataclasses), split_nodes_delimiter, regex extraction (takes the B13 regular_expressions handoff, adds the (?<!!) lookbehind as one KP), split_nodes_image/link, text_to_textnodes, markdown_to_blocks and block_to_block_type. markdown_syntax introduces only the HTML tags needed; general HTML belongs to the web batches (B16/B17). Nested inline styles and the CommonMark spec are out of scope. Reconciliation review: the markdown (7) and static_site_generation (8) topics follow Boot.dev's static site generator project chapter by chapter. Kept as topics, but they form one guided project and are best delivered as multisteps (a project track) rather than as 15 independent lessons.

static_site_generation.notes: HTMLNode/LeafNode/ParentNode (inheritance + recursion, as B08 recursion's note asked), text_node_to_html (match on enums), markdown_to_html_node, recursive static copy (shutil memorised), page generation with str.replace templates (Jinja is B17 lib_jinja) and the build/preview/basepath script. Boot.dev renders as ; kept for consistency with LeafNode. Unit tests use plain assert (unit_testing.unittest_module is optional, non-core). Project-shaped: the whole build is a good multistep built on these topics. Reconciliation review: the markdown (7) and static_site_generation (8) topics follow Boot.dev's static site generator project chapter by chapter. Kept as topics, but they form one guided project and are best delivered as multisteps (a project track) rather than as 15 independent lessons.

topics.title: Your first program: printing text
topics.summary: Write print("...") to display a line of text, use matching quotes, print blank lines, and recognise the typos that stop print from working.

knowledge_points.title: Print a line of text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hello, world!")
# Hello, world!
The text goes in quotes, inside the parentheses after print.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the exact output of one or two print calls; write the call that displays a given sentence.

knowledge_points.title: Single or double quotes, as long as they match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print('Hi there')
print("Hi there")
# Both print: Hi there
print('Hi there") is a SyntaxError: the quotes must match.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which of several print lines run and which are SyntaxErrors; fix a line with mismatched quotes.

knowledge_points.title: Each print starts a new line; print() alone prints a blank line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("one")
print()
print("two")
# one
#
# two  (the middle line is empty)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict multi-line output including blank lines; reorder print lines (Parsons) to produce a target output.

knowledge_points.title: Typos that break print
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Print("hi")    # NameError: Python names are case-sensitive
print "hi"     # SyntaxError: missing parentheses
print("hi"     # SyntaxError: "(" was never closed
knowledge_points.practice: For each line say 'prints' or 'error' and which error; fix three broken print lines.

topics.title: Printing numbers and several values at once
topics.summary: Print numbers, and pass several comma-separated values to one print call, which separates them with a space.

knowledge_points.title: Printing numbers without quotes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(42)
print("42")
# 42
# 42
Numbers need no quotes; both lines look the same on screen.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of prints with numbers and quoted digits; spot which line is a number and which is text.

knowledge_points.title: Several values in one print, separated by a space
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hello", "Ada")
# Hello Ada
Each comma-separated value is printed with one space between.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of print calls with 2-4 arguments; write one print that matches a target line.

knowledge_points.title: Mixing text and numbers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Age:", 36)
print("Total", 3, "items")
# Age: 36
# Total 3 items
knowledge_points.practice: Write print calls that combine a label and a number; predict the exact spacing.

knowledge_points.title: A comma inside quotes vs between arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a,b")
print("a", "b")
# a,b
# a b
Inside quotes a comma is just text; outside it separates values.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of look-alike pairs; fix a print that shows a stray comma or misses a space.

topics.title: Controlling separators and line endings: sep and end
topics.summary: Use print's sep= and end= keyword arguments to change what goes between values and what is printed after them.

knowledge_points.title: sep changes the separator
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("2026", "10", "12", sep="-")
# 2026-10-12
sep replaces the default single space.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output for different sep values; write a print that produces a dash- or slash-joined line.

knowledge_points.title: sep="" glues values together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("snow", "man", sep="")
# snowman
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output with sep=""; fix a print that leaves an unwanted space between values.

knowledge_points.title: end changes what comes after the line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Loading", end="...")
print("done")
# Loading...done
The default end is a newline; replacing it keeps the next print on the same line.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the combined output of two or three prints using end; fill in the end= value to join two lines.

knowledge_points.title: Combining sep and end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a", "b", sep="+", end="=")
print("ab")
# a+b=ab
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of prints using both arguments; write a print matching a target exactly.

topics.title: Laying out output with \n and \t
topics.summary: Put line breaks and tabs inside a printed string with the escape sequences \n and \t to lay out multi-line output from a single print.

knowledge_points.title: \n starts a new line inside one string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Roses\nViolets")
# Roses
# Violets
Backslash-n is one character: a line break.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many lines a print with \n produces and what is on each.

knowledge_points.title: Several prints vs one print with \n
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("a")
print("b")
print("a\nb")
# both produce a, then b on the next line
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite three print calls as one; decide which pairs of programs give identical output.

knowledge_points.title: \t lines text up in columns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Name\tScore")
print("Ada\t9")
Tabs jump to the next tab stop, so short columns line up.
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in escape sequences to build a two-column table; predict output containing tabs.

knowledge_points.title: Common slips: /n and blank lines
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("Hi/nthere")   # prints Hi/nthere: forward slash is not an escape
print("Hi\n")        # prints Hi then an empty line
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that use /n or produce an extra blank line; draw small text art from a single print.

topics.title: How a program runs: top to bottom, until an error
topics.summary: Predict what a program prints given that statements run in order, a SyntaxError stops everything before it starts, and a runtime error stops the program at that line; read the line number and error type in the message.

knowledge_points.title: Statements run top to bottom, one at a time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("first")
print("second")
print("third")
Output appears in exactly the order of the lines.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output order; reorder lines (Parsons) to print a target sequence.

knowledge_points.title: A SyntaxError means nothing runs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("one")
print("two"
print("three")
No output at all: Python checks the whole file before running any of it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output (or none) for files containing a syntax error on various lines.

knowledge_points.title: A runtime error stops at its line; earlier lines already ran
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print("one")
Print("two")
print("three")
# one
# NameError on line 2; line 3 never runs.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which lines print before the error; contrast with the SyntaxError case.

knowledge_points.title: Reading the error message: line number and error type
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "hello.py", line 2, in <module>
    Print("two")
NameError: name 'Print' is not defined
The last line names the error; "line 2" says where to look.
knowledge_points.practice: Given an error message, give the line number and error type; fix the line it points to.

topics.title: Running a .py file from the terminal
topics.summary: Run a saved script with python3 file.py from the right folder, fix the 'can't open file' error, and re-run after editing.

knowledge_points.title: python3 hello.py runs the file
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 hello.py
Hello, world!
The terminal runs every line of hello.py and shows its output.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the command that runs a named file; predict the terminal output for a given hello.py.

knowledge_points.title: You must be in the folder that holds the file
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 hello.py
python3: can't open file '/Users/ada/hello.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory
$ cd projects
