knowledge_points.title: Functions can change the caller's dict
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the caller's dict after calls; choose between mutating and returning a new dict.

knowledge_points.title: Don't add or delete keys while looping over the dict
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a cleanup loop; predict which loops raise RuntimeError (adding/deleting keys vs updating values).

topics.title: Sets: unique values and fast membership
topics.summary: Create a set from a literal or a list to remove duplicates, test membership, and avoid the {} and indexing pitfalls.

knowledge_points.title: A set keeps each value once
knowledge_points.worked_example:
s = {3, 1, 3, 2, 1}
print(len(s))       # 3
print(sorted(s))    # [1, 2, 3]
Duplicates are dropped; a set has no fixed order, so sort it when you need to display it in order.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() of set literals with repeats; predict sorted() of a set.

knowledge_points.title: set(list) removes duplicates
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['hi', 'yo', 'hi', 'hi']
print(len(set(words)))  # 2
print(sorted(set('banana')))  # ['a', 'b', 'n']
Converting to a set is the quick way to count or list the distinct values.
knowledge_points.practice: Write an expression counting distinct items; predict the distinct letters of a word.

knowledge_points.title: Empty set is set(), not {}
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(type({}))     # <class 'dict'>
print(type(set()))  # <class 'set'>
print({'a'} == set('a'))  # True
{} is an empty dict; braces only make a set when they contain values.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that starts a set with {} and then calls add; multiple choice on the type of brace expressions.

knowledge_points.title: Membership yes, indexing no
knowledge_points.worked_example:
vowels = {'a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u'}
print('e' in vowels)  # True
print(vowels[0])  # TypeError: 'set' object is not subscriptable
Sets answer 'is it in here?' quickly but have no positions.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict in tests and the indexing error; choose list or set for described tasks.

topics.title: Adding and removing set items
topics.summary: Grow a set with add(), remove items with remove() or discard(), and use a 'seen' set to find or drop duplicates.

knowledge_points.title: add() ignores values already present
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tags = set()
tags.add('red')
tags.add('blue')
tags.add('red')
print(len(tags))  # 2
Adding a duplicate is not an error; it just changes nothing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the size after a sequence of adds; write a loop adding every word of a list.

knowledge_points.title: remove() vs discard()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
tags = {'red', 'blue'}
tags.discard('green')   # no error
tags.remove('green')    # KeyError: 'green'
remove insists the value is there; discard quietly does nothing if it is not.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which line errors; choose remove or discard for a described task.

knowledge_points.title: A 'seen' set finds repeats
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the seen-set loop; write a function returning True if a list has any duplicate.

knowledge_points.title: Remove duplicates but keep the order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
seen = set()
result = []
for x in [4, 7, 4, 1, 7]:
    if x not in seen:
        seen.add(x)
        result.append(x)
print(result)  # [4, 7, 1]
set(lst) loses the order; a seen set plus a result list keeps first appearances in order.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the order-preserving dedupe; fix a version that appends before checking.

topics.title: Combining sets: union, intersection and difference
topics.summary: Use |, &, - and ^ (and their method names) to combine sets, and test subsets and same-items-in-any-order.

knowledge_points.title: Union | : in either
knowledge_points.practice: Predict unions; write the union of two given sets.

knowledge_points.title: Intersection & : in both
knowledge_points.practice: Predict intersections; write code that finds common items of two lists via sets.

knowledge_points.title: Difference - and symmetric difference ^
knowledge_points.practice: Predict differences in both directions; choose the operator for described questions.

knowledge_points.title: Subsets and order-free equality
knowledge_points.practice: Predict subset and equality tests; write a check that a recipe's ingredients are all available.

topics.title: Lists of lists: grids
topics.summary: Read and change cells of a 2D list with grid[row][col], get its size, and loop over all cells with nested loops.

knowledge_points.title: Double indexing: row, then column
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3],
        [4, 5, 6]]
print(grid[1])     # [4, 5, 6]
print(grid[1][0])  # 4
grid[r] is a whole row (a list); grid[r][c] is one cell in it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict single and double indexing; write the expression for a described cell, including negative indexes.

knowledge_points.title: Changing a cell and measuring the grid
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
grid[0][2] = 7
print(grid)          # [[0, 0, 7], [0, 0, 0]]
print(len(grid), len(grid[0]))  # 2 3
len(grid) is the number of rows; len(grid[0]) the number of columns.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the grid after cell assignments; fix code that swaps row and column (IndexError).

knowledge_points.title: Nested for over rows and values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
total = 0
for row in grid:
    for value in row:
        total += value
print(total)  # 21
The outer loop hands you each row list; the inner loop walks along it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a grid total or count; predict how many times the inner body runs.

knowledge_points.title: Nested range loops when you need positions
knowledge_points.practice: Write a search returning the (row, col) of a value; reorder the nested index loop lines.

topics.title: Working with grid rows, columns and diagonals
topics.summary: Compute row sums, extract a column, walk a diagonal and transpose a grid, as in tic-tac-toe and sudoku checks.

knowledge_points.title: A row is a list: sum or check it directly
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
for row in grid:
    print(sum(row))
# 6
# 15
Built-ins that work on lists work on each row.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict row sums and maxima; write a check that every row has the same sum.

knowledge_points.title: A column needs one item from every row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
col = []
for row in grid:
    col.append(row[1])
print(col)  # [2, 5]
There is no grid[:][1]; collect row[c] from each row.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a column extractor; fix code that uses grid[1] when it meant column 1.

knowledge_points.title: Diagonals: the row and column index move together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
board = [['X', 'O', 'O'],
         ['O', 'X', 'O'],
         ['O', 'O', 'X']]
diag = []
for i in range(3):
    diag.append(board[i][i])
print(diag)  # ['X', 'X', 'X']
The main diagonal is board[i][i]; the other one is board[i][2 - i].
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the index for the anti-diagonal; write a tic-tac-toe win check for diagonals.

knowledge_points.title: Transposing: rows become columns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
flipped = []
for c in range(len(grid[0])):
    new_row = []
    for row in grid:
        new_row.append(row[c])
    flipped.append(new_row)
print(flipped)  # [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
Each column of the old grid becomes a row of the new one; a 2x3 grid becomes 3x2.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the transpose lines; predict the shape and contents of a transposed grid.

topics.title: Lists of dictionaries as records
topics.summary: Store records as a list of dicts, read fields inside a loop, filter records, find the best by a field, and add a new record.

knowledge_points.title: Index the list, then the key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = [{'name': 'Ana', 'age': 31},
          {'name': 'Bo', 'age': 27}]
print(people[1]['name'])  # Bo
people[1] is a dict; ['name'] then looks inside it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict two-step lookups; write the expression for a described field of a described record.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over records and read fields
knowledge_points.practice: Write a filter that prints matching names; fix a loop that writes people['age'] instead of p['age'].

knowledge_points.title: Best record by a field
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = [{'name': 'Ana', 'age': 31}, {'name': 'Bo', 'age': 27}]
oldest = people[0]
for p in people:
    if p['age'] > oldest['age']:
        oldest = p
print(oldest['name'])  # Ana
Keep the whole best record, not just its number, so you can report any field.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the youngest/highest-scoring search; predict output with a tie.

knowledge_points.title: Adding a record and missing fields
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = [{'name': 'Ana', 'age': 31}]
people.append({'name': 'Cy'})
for p in people:
    print(p['name'], p.get('age', '?'))
# Ana 31
# Cy ?
append a new dict; records may lack a field, so read optional fields with get.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code appending a record built from input values; fix a loop that crashes on a record missing a key.

topics.title: Dicts holding lists and dicts
topics.summary: Look up and update values inside a dict of lists (gradebook) and a dict of dicts (profiles), and loop over them.

knowledge_points.title: A dict of lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grades = {'ana': [90, 85], 'bo': [70]}
print(grades['ana'])     # [90, 85]
print(grades['ana'][1])  # 85
print(sum(grades['ana']) / len(grades['ana']))  # 87.5
The key picks a list; then index or use list built-ins on it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lookups and averages; write the average for a named student.

knowledge_points.title: Appending to an inner list
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict after appends; fix grades['bo'] = 88 that replaced the list.

knowledge_points.title: A dict of dicts
knowledge_points.practice: Predict nested lookups and updates; write the update for a described change.

knowledge_points.title: Looping over a dict of dicts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
people = {'ana': {'age': 31, 'city': 'Oslo'},
          'bo': {'age': 27, 'city': 'Lima'}}
for name, info in people.items():
    print(name, 'lives in', info['city'])
# ana lives in Oslo
# bo lives in Lima
items() gives each outer key with its inner dict; read fields from the inner dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the loop lines; write a loop that prints everyone over a given age.

topics.title: Finding your way through deeply nested data
topics.summary: Follow a path of keys and indexes through JSON-shaped data, loop over a list inside a dict, and tell from the error which step failed.

knowledge_points.title: Read a path one step at a time
knowledge_points.practice: Write the access path for a described value; trace the type after each step.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over the list you reach
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop printing a field from each item of a nested list; predict its output.

knowledge_points.title: Which step went wrong?
knowledge_points.practice: Match each failing path to its error; fix paths that skip a list level.

knowledge_points.title: Defaults at each level with get
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = {'meta': {'page': 2}}
print(data.get('meta', {}).get('page', 1))   # 2
print(data.get('extra', {}).get('page', 1))  # 1
A default of {} lets the next get run safely when an optional level is missing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict chained get results; rewrite a crashing path with get defaults.

topics.title: match on the shape of data: sequence and mapping patterns
topics.summary: Use case patterns that match lists by length and contents ([x, y], [first, *rest]) and dicts by keys ({'type': t}).

knowledge_points.title: Sequence patterns match length and items
knowledge_points.worked_example:
command = 'go north'.split()
match command:
    case ['go', direction]:
        print('going', direction)  # going north
    case ['quit']:
        print('bye')
A list pattern matches only a list of exactly that length; literals must be equal, names capture.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which case runs for several commands; write a case for a two-word command.

knowledge_points.title: A star collects the rest
knowledge_points.worked_example:
command = ['drop', 'key', 'map']
match command:
    case ['drop', *items]:
        print(items)  # ['key', 'map']
*name matches any number of items, including none, just like star unpacking.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the captured list (including empty); fix a pattern that fails because the length is fixed.

knowledge_points.title: Mapping patterns match keys
knowledge_points.worked_example:
event = {'type': 'click', 'x': 3, 'y': 4}
match event:
    case {'type': 'key', 'key': k}:
        print('key', k)
    case {'type': 'click', 'x': x, 'y': y}:
        print('click at', x, y)  # click at 3 4
A dict pattern needs the listed keys with matching values; extra keys in the data are allowed.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which case runs for several events; write a mapping pattern for a described event.

knowledge_points.title: Order of cases and the fallback
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for cmd in [['look'], ['go'], ['go', 'up', 'now']]:
    match cmd:
        case ['go', where]:
            print('go', where)
        case [verb]:
            print('just', verb)
        case _:
            print('unknown')
# just look
# just go
# unknown
Cases are tried top to bottom; ['go'] fails the 2-item pattern but matches [verb].
knowledge_points.practice: Predict outputs for a list of inputs; reorder cases so a specific pattern is not shadowed.

topics.title: List comprehensions: transforming every item
topics.summary: Replace a loop-and-append with [expression for item in iterable] to build a new list from each item.

knowledge_points.title: From loop-and-append to a comprehension
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
squares = []
for n in nums:
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)                # [1, 4, 9]
print([n * n for n in nums])  # [1, 4, 9]
The comprehension packs the loop and the append into one expression: what to keep, then the for.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite short append loops as comprehensions; fill in the expression part of a comprehension.

knowledge_points.title: Any expression, any iterable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['hi', 'there']
print([w.upper() for w in words])    # ['HI', 'THERE']
print([len(w) for w in words])       # [2, 5]
print([i * 10 for i in range(4)])    # [0, 10, 20, 30]
Method calls, functions and arithmetic all work; strings and ranges work as the source too.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict comprehension results over lists, strings and ranges.

knowledge_points.title: A comprehension builds a new list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
prices = [10, 20]
with_tax = [p * 1.5 for p in prices]
print(prices, with_tax)  # [10, 20] [15.0, 30.0]
The original list is untouched; assign the result to keep it.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that writes a comprehension but never assigns it; predict both lists afterwards.

knowledge_points.title: Parsing text into numbers in one line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = '3 14 15'
nums = [int(x) for x in line.split()]
print(nums, sum(nums))  # [3, 14, 15] 32
split gives strings; the comprehension converts each one.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the parse line for comma- or space-separated numbers; fix a version that sums strings.

topics.title: Filtering in a comprehension, and if-else inside one
topics.summary: Keep only matching items with a trailing if, combine filtering with a transform, and tell it apart from an if-else expression at the front.

knowledge_points.title: A trailing if keeps only matching items
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7, -3]
print([n for n in nums if n > 0])  # [4, 7]
Items whose condition is False are skipped; the result may be shorter.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict filtered lists; write a comprehension keeping even numbers.

knowledge_points.title: Filter and transform together
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['a', 'tree', 'is', 'green']
print([w.upper() for w in words if len(w) > 2])  # ['TREE', 'GREEN']
The if decides which items survive; the front expression decides what is stored for each survivor.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the parts of a comprehension (Parsons on tokens); write one from a described loop with if and append.

knowledge_points.title: if-else at the front changes values, keeps every item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7]
print(['pos' if n > 0 else 'neg' for n in nums])  # ['pos', 'neg', 'pos']
print([n if n > 0 else 0 for n in nums])          # [4, 0, 7]
A conditional expression before for picks a value for every item, so the length never changes.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results and their lengths; choose between front if-else and trailing if for described tasks.

knowledge_points.title: else at the end is a syntax error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7]
print([n for n in nums if n > 0 else 0])  # SyntaxError: invalid syntax
A trailing if cannot have else; move the if-else in front of for if every item should get a value.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix misplaced if-else comprehensions; predict which comprehensions are valid.

topics.title: Comprehensions with sum(), any() and all()
topics.summary: Feed comprehensions to sum/max/min, answer 'any?' and 'all?' questions with any() and all(), and know their empty-list results.

knowledge_points.title: Totals, maxima and counts in one line
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['hi', 'there', 'you']
print(sum([len(w) for w in words]))   # 10
print(max([len(w) for w in words]))   # 5
print(sum([1 for w in words if 'h' in w]))  # 2
Build the list of numbers you want, then hand it to a built-in. Summing 1 for each match counts matches.
knowledge_points.practice: Write one-line totals and counts; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: any() and all() replace search flags
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [4, -1, 7]
print(any([n < 0 for n in nums]))  # True
print(all([n < 0 for n in nums]))  # False
any is True if at least one value is True; all only if every one is. They replace the found = False loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a flag loop with any or all; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Empty lists: any is False, all is True
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(any([]))  # False
print(all([]))  # True
print(all([n > 0 for n in []]))  # True
'Every one of nothing' is vacuously true; guard with a length check if an empty input should fail.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict any/all on empty and filtered-to-empty lists; fix a validator that accepts an empty list.

topics.title: Comprehensions over grids: nested and two-for comprehensions
topics.summary: Pull a column or row totals from a grid, build a grid safely, flatten a grid and build pairs with two for clauses.

knowledge_points.title: One comprehension over the rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print([row[0] for row in grid])   # [1, 4]
print([sum(row) for row in grid])  # [6, 15]
Each item is a row, so the expression can index or sum it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write comprehensions for a column and for row maxima; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Building a grid with a comprehension
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
grid[0][0] = 1
print(grid)  # [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
Each pass makes a fresh row, so changing one cell does not change the others (unlike [[0] * 3] * 2).
knowledge_points.practice: Write a comprehension for an h-by-w grid of a given value; fix grid code built with * on the outer list.

knowledge_points.title: Two for clauses flatten a grid
knowledge_points.worked_example:
grid = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print([x for row in grid for x in row])  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
The for clauses read in the same order as nested loops: outer first, inner second.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the clauses to match a given nested loop; predict flattened results.

knowledge_points.title: Pairs from two loops, with a filter
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print([(a, b) for a in range(3) for b in range(3) if a < b])
# [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]
Every combination of a and b is tried; the if keeps the ones you want. Past two clauses, a plain loop is clearer.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the pairs produced; write a comprehension for all pairs with a given sum.

topics.title: Dictionary comprehensions: building a dict in one line
topics.summary: Write {key: value for item in iterable}, including from two lists with zip and with a filter, and predict what happens when keys repeat.

knowledge_points.title: Key and value from each item
knowledge_points.practice: Predict dict comprehensions; rewrite an empty-dict-and-assign loop as one.

knowledge_points.title: Keys and values from two lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['ana', 'bo']
ages = [31, 27]
print({n: a for n, a in zip(names, ages)})  # {'ana': 31, 'bo': 27}
Unpack each zipped pair; the comprehension can then transform either side (dict(zip()) cannot).
knowledge_points.practice: Write a comprehension mapping names to upper-case names or doubled values; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Filtering with a trailing if
knowledge_points.practice: Predict filtered dict comprehensions; fill in the condition for a described filter.

knowledge_points.title: Repeated keys: the last one wins
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results with repeated keys; choose between a dict comprehension and grouping for described tasks.

topics.title: Transforming and filtering dicts, and set comprehensions
topics.summary: Build a new dict from an existing one's items (change values, filter by value, swap keys and values) and write set comprehensions.

knowledge_points.title: Changing every value
knowledge_points.practice: Write a comprehension applying a discount; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Keeping entries that pass a test
knowledge_points.practice: Write a filter by value or by key; fix a loop that deletes entries while iterating by rewriting it as a comprehension.

knowledge_points.title: Swapping keys and values
knowledge_points.practice: Predict inversions with unique and repeated values; choose comprehension or grouping.

knowledge_points.title: Set comprehensions: braces without a colon
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ['Hi', 'hi', 'Yo']
print(sorted({w.lower() for w in words}))  # ['hi', 'yo']
print(type({w: 1 for w in words}))  # <class 'dict'>
{expr for ...} builds a set (duplicates dropped); {k: v for ...} builds a dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each comprehension makes a set, dict or list and its contents; write a set comprehension of distinct first letters.

topics.title: Stacks: last in, first out with a list
topics.summary: Use a list as a stack with append() and pop(), peek and test for empty safely, and solve bracket matching with a stack.

knowledge_points.title: Push with append, pop from the end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
stack = []
stack.append('a')
stack.append('b')
stack.append('c')
print(stack.pop())  # c
print(stack)        # ['a', 'b']
The last item pushed is the first popped (LIFO), like a stack of plates.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict pop results after a sequence of pushes and pops; trace the stack contents.

knowledge_points.title: Peek and check for empty before popping
knowledge_points.worked_example:
stack = ['a']
print(stack[-1])  # a  (peek, nothing removed)
stack.pop()
if stack:
    print('more')
else:
    print('empty')  # empty
stack.pop()  # IndexError: pop from empty list
stack[-1] looks without removing; test with if stack: before popping.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that pops an empty stack; predict outputs with peek vs pop.

knowledge_points.title: Undo: popping reverses the order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
history = []
for action in ['type', 'bold', 'delete']:
    history.append(action)
while history:
    print('undo', history.pop())
# undo delete
# undo bold
# undo type
Popping everything gives the items back newest first: the basis of undo and reversing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict an undo sequence; write a function reversing a string with a stack.

knowledge_points.title: Matching brackets with a stack
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the stack on a given string; fix a version that forgets the final empty check.

topics.title: Queues: first in, first out with deque
topics.summary: Model a FIFO queue, see why list.pop(0) is the slow way, and use collections.deque with append(), popleft() and maxlen.

knowledge_points.title: FIFO: serve in arrival order
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = ['ana', 'bo']
line.append('cy')
print(line.pop(0))  # ana
print(line)         # ['bo', 'cy']
Join at the back, leave from the front. pop(0) works, but every remaining item shifts down one place.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict who is served after a sequence of joins and serves; multiple choice on stack vs queue for described situations.

knowledge_points.title: deque: a queue built for both ends
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import deque
q = deque(['ana', 'bo'])
q.append('cy')
print(q.popleft())  # ana
print(q)            # deque(['bo', 'cy'])
popleft() removes from the front without shifting, so it stays fast for long queues. Copy the import line as given.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a list queue using deque; predict q after mixed append/popleft.

knowledge_points.title: Process until the queue is empty
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import deque
jobs = deque(['print', 'save'])
while jobs:
    job = jobs.popleft()
    print('doing', job)
    if job == 'print':
        jobs.append('log')
# doing print
# doing save
# doing log
while jobs: stops when nothing is left; new work added during the loop joins the back.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the queue through a processing loop; predict the order of work.

knowledge_points.title: appendleft and maxlen: keep only the latest
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import deque
recent = deque(maxlen=3)
for page in ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']:
    recent.append(page)
print(list(recent))  # ['b', 'c', 'd']
recent.appendleft('z')
print(list(recent))  # ['z', 'b', 'c']
With maxlen, adding to a full deque drops an item from the other end.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict contents of a bounded deque; write a 'last 5 entries' history.

topics.title: Counting with collections.Counter
topics.summary: Count items with Counter, read counts (missing is 0), get the most common with most_common(), and add more counts.

knowledge_points.title: Counter counts any iterable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter('banana')
print(c['a'], c['n'], c['z'])  # 3 2 0
One call replaces the counting loop; a missing key reads as 0 instead of raising KeyError.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts including missing keys; rewrite a get(k, 0) counting loop with Counter.

knowledge_points.title: most_common(n) for the top n
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
words = 'the cat and the hat and the bat'.split()
print(Counter(words).most_common(2))  # [('the', 3), ('and', 2)]
Returns (item, count) pairs, biggest first: the sort-by-value work done for you.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict most_common results; write a top-3 report with unpacking.

knowledge_points.title: Adding more counts with update() and +
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter(['a', 'b'])
c.update(['a', 'c'])
print(c['a'])  # 2
print((Counter('ab') + Counter('bc'))['b'])  # 2
update adds counts (unlike dict.update, which replaces values); + combines two Counters.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts after update and +; multiple choice contrasting Counter.update with dict.update.

knowledge_points.title: A Counter is still a dict
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter('aab')
for ch, n in c.items():
    print(ch, n)
# a 2
# b 1
print(len(c), 'a' in c, 'z' in c)  # 2 True False
Loops, len and in work as on a dict; reading c['z'] gives 0 but does not add 'z'.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict loops and membership on a Counter; fix code that expects c['z'] to raise KeyError.

topics.title: Automatic defaults with collections.defaultdict
topics.summary: Count with defaultdict(int) and group with defaultdict(list), and know that reading a missing key creates it.

knowledge_points.title: defaultdict(int) for counting
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a get(k, 0) counter with defaultdict; predict the counts.

knowledge_points.title: defaultdict(list) for grouping
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a setdefault grouping loop; predict the groups.

knowledge_points.title: Pass the type, don't call it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import defaultdict
ok = defaultdict(list)
bad = defaultdict(list())  # TypeError: first argument must be callable or None
defaultdict needs something it can call later to make each default: list, int, set, not list().
knowledge_points.practice: Fix broken defaultdict constructions; choose int, list or set for described tasks.

knowledge_points.title: Reading a missing key adds it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import defaultdict
d = defaultdict(int)
print(d['x'])     # 0
print(dict(d))    # {'x': 0}
print('y' in d)   # False
Unlike get, looking up creates the entry; test with in when you only want to check.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict after lookups; fix a check that accidentally adds keys.

topics.title: Records with named fields: namedtuple
topics.summary: Define a namedtuple type, read fields by name, use it like a tuple, and make changed copies with _replace().

knowledge_points.title: Define a record type and read fields by name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(3, 4)
print(p.x, p.y)  # 3 4
print(p)         # Point(x=3, y=4)
p.x reads better than p[0] and prints with its field names.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict field access and printing; write a namedtuple definition for a described record.

knowledge_points.title: Still a tuple: index, unpack, compare, cannot change
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(3, 4)
x, y = p
print(p[0], x, p == (3, 4))  # 3 3 True
p.x = 5  # AttributeError: can't set attribute
Everything a tuple does still works; fields are read-only.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict tuple operations on a namedtuple; fix code that assigns to a field.

knowledge_points.title: A list of named records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Pet = namedtuple('Pet', ['name', 'age'])
pets = [Pet('Rex', 3), Pet('Tom', 5)]
for pet in pets:
    if pet.age > 4:
        print(pet.name)  # Tom
Replaces lists of plain tuples where you had to remember which position meant what.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite an index-based loop over tuples with field names; predict outputs.

knowledge_points.title: Keyword creation and _replace()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(x=1, y=2)
q = p._replace(y=9)
print(p, q)  # Point(x=1, y=2) Point(x=1, y=9)
_replace returns a new record with some fields changed; the original stays the same.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both records after _replace; write code moving a point one step right.

topics.title: Every combination: product, combinations and permutations
topics.summary: Replace nested loops with itertools.product, and list unordered pairs with combinations and ordered arrangements with permutations.

knowledge_points.title: product() replaces nested loops
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import product
print(list(product([1, 2], 'ab')))
# [(1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
Same tuples, same order as a loop over 1, 2 with an inner loop over 'a', 'b'. list() shows the results.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a two-level nested loop with product; predict the tuples.

knowledge_points.title: combinations(): unordered picks, no repeats
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import combinations
for a, b in combinations(['ana', 'bo', 'cy'], 2):
    print(a, 'vs', b)
# ana vs bo
# ana vs cy
# bo vs cy
Each pair appears once, like a loop where the inner index starts after the outer one.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict pairs; write a schedule of matches for a list of players.

knowledge_points.title: permutations(): order matters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import permutations
print(list(permutations('abc', 2)))
# [('a', 'b'), ('a', 'c'), ('b', 'a'), ('b', 'c'), ('c', 'a'), ('c', 'b')]
('a', 'b') and ('b', 'a') are different arrangements, so there are twice as many as combinations.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict permutations of short inputs; count them with len(list(...)).

knowledge_points.title: Which tool for which question?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import combinations, permutations, product
print(len(list(product('HT', repeat=3))))     # 8
print(len(list(combinations(range(5), 2))))  # 10
print(len(list(permutations(range(5), 2))))  # 20
Repeats allowed: product. Choose a group: combinations. Order a line-up: permutations.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the right function for word problems and give the count.

topics.title: Joining and stretching iterables: chain, count and zip_longest
topics.summary: Loop over several lists in a row with chain, number things endlessly with count, and handle lists of different lengths with zip_longest or zip(strict=True).

knowledge_points.title: chain(): one loop over several lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import chain
total = 0
for x in chain([1, 2], [3, 4]):
    total += x
print(total)  # 10
print(list(chain([1, 2], 'ab')))  # [1, 2, 'a', 'b']
No new combined list is built; items come from each input in turn.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict chained output; rewrite two loops over two lists as one loop with chain.

knowledge_points.title: count(): an endless counter
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import count
for n in count(10, 5):
    if n > 25:
        break
    print(n)
# 10
# 15
# 20
# 25
count never stops by itself; pair it with break (or zip) to end the loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output; fix a count loop that never ends.

knowledge_points.title: zip stops early; zip_longest fills the gaps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from itertools import zip_longest
names = ['ana', 'bo', 'cy']
scores = [90, 80]
print(list(zip(names, scores)))  # [('ana', 90), ('bo', 80)]
print(list(zip_longest(names, scores, fillvalue=0)))
# [('ana', 90), ('bo', 80), ('cy', 0)]
Plain zip silently drops the extra item; zip_longest keeps it and pads with fillvalue (None by default).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict both results for uneven lists; choose which to use.

knowledge_points.title: zip(strict=True) refuses uneven lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
names = ['ana', 'bo', 'cy']
scores = [90, 80]
print(list(zip(names, scores, strict=True)))
# ValueError: zip() argument 2 is shorter than argument 1
When lengths should match, strict=True turns a silent bug into an error.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise ValueError; fix code that silently lost data.

topics.title: Functions are values: naming, storing and printing them
topics.summary: Treat a function as a value: give it a second name, keep functions in a list and loop over them, and tell f (the function) from f() (its result).

knowledge_points.title: A second name for the same function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def shout(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"

yell = shout
print(yell("hi"))  # HI!
yell = shout copies no code: both names now refer to the same function object.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what calls through a second name return; fill in the assignment that makes a new name work.

knowledge_points.title: f is the function, f() is its result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len("abc"))  # 3
print(len)  # <built-in function len>
result = len
print(result)  # <built-in function len>
Without parentheses nothing is called: you get the function itself.
knowledge_points.practice: For each line, decide whether it prints a result or a function object.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting the parentheses is a silent bug
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the missing call in short snippets that print the wrong answer.

knowledge_points.title: Keeping functions in a list
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of looping over a list of functions; write a loop that applies each function in a list to one value.

topics.title: Functions in a dictionary: dispatch tables
topics.summary: Store functions as dictionary values, pick and call one by key (for example from user input), replace an if/elif chain on a string with a lookup and a default, and keep every function in the table callable the same way.

knowledge_points.title: Functions as dictionary values
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of calls through a dict of functions; add an entry for a new operation.

knowledge_points.title: Choose the function from what the user types
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the calculator for several inputs, including an unknown symbol; write the lookup-and-call lines.

knowledge_points.title: Replace an if/elif chain with a lookup and a default
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite an elif chain that compares one string as a dispatch table; predict get() with and without a default.

knowledge_points.title: Same arguments for every entry; store the function, not its result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def square(n):
    return n * n
operations = {"square": square, "add": add}
print(operations["add"](2, 3))  # 5
operations["square"](2, 3)  # TypeError: square() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given
{"square": square()}  # TypeError: square() missing 1 required positional argument: 'n'
The caller treats every entry alike, so every function must accept the same arguments; square() would call it while building the dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the entry that breaks the table and fix its parameters; fix a table that stores call results.

topics.title: Sorting and choosing with your own key function
topics.summary: Pass your own function as key= to sorted(), max() and min(), including tie-breaking keys that return a tuple.

knowledge_points.title: key= with a function you wrote
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def last_letter(word):
    return word[-1]

print(sorted(["plum", "kiwi", "fig"], key=last_letter))
# ['fig', 'kiwi', 'plum']
sorted calls last_letter on every item and orders by the results g, i, m.

knowledge_points.title: Key functions for records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def price(item):
    return item[1]

items = [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5), ("jam", 2)]
print(sorted(items, key=price))
# [('jam', 2), ('tea', 3), ('cake', 5)]
The key picks the field to sort by; the records themselves are returned whole.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the key function that sorts records by a named field, then sort in reverse with reverse=True.

knowledge_points.title: max() and min() with key= return the item, not the key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def price(item):
    return item[1]

items = [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5), ("jam", 2)]
print(max(items, key=price))  # ('cake', 5)
print(min(items, key=price)[0])  # jam
The key is only used to compare; you get back the whole record.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict max/min results with a key; fix code that expects max to return the key value.

topics.title: Transforming and selecting with map() and filter()
topics.summary: Use map() to apply a function to every item and filter() to keep the items that pass a test, converting the lazy result with list().

knowledge_points.title: map() applies a function to every item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

print(list(map(double, [1, 2, 3])))  # [2, 4, 6]
print(list(map(int, ["4", "5"])))  # [4, 5]
map(f, items) does the job of a loop that appends f(item) for every item.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict map results; rewrite an append loop as list(map(...)).

knowledge_points.title: map() gives a map object that is used up once
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

m = map(double, [1, 2])
print(list(m))  # [2, 4]
print(list(m))  # []
print(m) would show <map object at 0x...>; the values are produced on demand and only once.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a second list() or loop over the same map object gives; fix code that prints a map object.

knowledge_points.title: filter() keeps the items that pass a test
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0

print(list(filter(is_even, range(10))))  # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
filter calls the test on each item and keeps those where it returns True.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict filter results; write a test function and a filter call for a stated condition.

knowledge_points.title: Parsing a line with map(), then filtering
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = "3 8 1 6"
numbers = list(map(int, line.split()))
print(numbers)  # [3, 8, 1, 6]
print(list(filter(is_even, numbers)))  # [8, 6]
map(int, text.split()) is the standard way to parse numbers from one line of input; filter then keeps the ones you want (is_even from KP3).
knowledge_points.practice: Parse lines of numbers with map(int, ...split()); chain a filter on the result; fill in the missing function names.

topics.title: Writing small functions with lambda
topics.summary: Write lambda expressions with one or more parameters, know the body is a single expression that is returned, and pass a lambda straight into a call.

knowledge_points.title: lambda parameters: expression
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

double_too = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(5), double_too(5))  # 10 10
A lambda is an unnamed function; the expression after the colon is returned.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert one-line defs to lambdas and back; predict calls to a lambda.

knowledge_points.title: Several parameters, or none
knowledge_points.worked_example:
add = lambda a, b: a + b
print(add(2, 3))  # 5
get_answer = lambda: 42
print(get_answer())  # 42
Parameters are separated by commas, exactly as in def; a lambda with no parameters is still called with ().
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of multi-parameter lambdas; write a lambda for a given two-input formula.

knowledge_points.title: One expression only: use a conditional expression for choices
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sign = lambda n: "negative" if n < 0 else "not negative"
print(sign(-4))  # negative
bad = lambda x: return x  # SyntaxError: invalid syntax
No statements (return, if blocks, assignments) are allowed in a lambda body; x if c else y is an expression, so it is.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which lambdas are valid; rewrite an if/else def as a lambda with a conditional expression.

knowledge_points.title: Passing a lambda straight into a call
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a lambda argument so a call produces a target value; predict calls of apply-style helpers with lambdas.

topics.title: Lambdas as sort keys and with map() and filter()
topics.summary: Use lambdas inline as key= for sorted/max/min and as the function for map() and filter(), and know when a named def is clearer.

knowledge_points.title: key=lambda to sort records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
items = [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5), ("jam", 2)]
print(sorted(items, key=lambda item: item[1]))
# [('jam', 2), ('tea', 3), ('cake', 5)]
The lambda replaces a one-line key function defined elsewhere.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the key=lambda that sorts by a named field or computed value; predict the resulting order.

knowledge_points.title: max() and min() with a lambda key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [("ana", 81), ("bo", 92), ("cy", 77)]
best = max(scores, key=lambda s: s[1])
print(best[0])  # bo
Remember max returns the whole record; index it afterwards for the part you want.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the best/worst record by a field; fix code that indexes the wrong part of the result.

knowledge_points.title: Lambdas with map() and filter()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["hi", "hello", "hey", "howdy"]
print(list(filter(lambda w: len(w) > 3, words)))  # ['hello', 'howdy']
print(list(map(lambda w: w[0].upper(), words)))  # ['H', 'H', 'H', 'H']
filter's lambda must return True/False; map's lambda returns the new value.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict map/filter calls with lambdas; write one that keeps or transforms items by a rule.

knowledge_points.title: When a def is clearer than a lambda
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, -1, 4]
print(list(filter(lambda n: n if n > 0, nums)))  # SyntaxError: expected 'else' after 'if' expression
A lambda cannot hold an if statement; once logic needs several steps or a name worth reading, write a def.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix broken lambdas; choose between lambda and def for described tasks.

topics.title: Functions inside functions and the enclosing scope
topics.summary: Define a helper inside another function, read the outer function's variables from it, and predict name lookup with the LEGB rule.

knowledge_points.title: A def inside a def
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet_all():
    def greet(name):
        print("Hi", name)
    greet("Ana")
    greet("Bo")

greet_all()  # Hi Ana / Hi Bo
The inner def runs each time greet_all runs, creating a helper only greet_all uses.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output and call order for nested defs.

knowledge_points.title: The inner function can read the outer function's variables
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results when an inner function reads outer variables and parameters.

knowledge_points.title: The inner function does not exist outside
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which calls work and which raise NameError.

knowledge_points.practice: Predict which of several same-named variables a line reads; fix a program that shadowed a built-in.

topics.title: Returning functions: closures and function factories
topics.summary: Write a function that builds and returns another function which remembers values from where it was made, and avoid the late-binding trap.

knowledge_points.title: Return the inner function itself
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_greeter(greeting):
    def greet(name):
        return f"{greeting}, {name}!"
    return greet

hello = make_greeter("Hello")
print(hello("Ana"))  # Hello, Ana!
return greet (no parentheses) hands back the function; it still knows greeting after make_greeter has finished.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict calls to returned functions; fix a factory that returns greet() instead of greet.

knowledge_points.title: Each call makes a separate closure
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_multiplier(n):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * n
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
triple = make_multiplier(3)
print(double(5), triple(5))  # 10 15
Each call of make_multiplier has its own n, and each returned function remembers its own.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results from several functions made by one factory; write a factory for a described family of functions.

knowledge_points.title: Returning a lambda
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_adder(n):
    return lambda x: x + n

add5 = make_adder(5)
print(add5(10))  # 15
print(make_adder(1)(1))  # 2
A lambda closes over n just like a def; make_adder(1)(1) builds and calls in one line.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite def-based factories with lambdas; predict chained calls like f(a)(b).

knowledge_points.title: Late binding: closures see the variable, not its old value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 2
times_n = lambda x: x * n
n = 10
print(times_n(3))  # 30, not 6

m = 2
times_m = lambda x, m=m: x * m
m = 10
print(times_m(3))  # 6
times_n reads n when it is called, not when it was made; a default m=m freezes the value at creation, because defaults are computed once.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results when a captured variable changes after the function is made (including functions made in a loop); fix the bug with a default argument or a factory call.

topics.title: Closures that remember state with nonlocal
topics.summary: Use nonlocal to update a variable of the enclosing function, build independent counters, and know when mutation needs no nonlocal.

knowledge_points.title: nonlocal lets the inner function rebind an outer variable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def counter():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter

c = make_counter()
print(c(), c(), c())  # 1 2 3
count lives on between calls because the closure keeps it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values returned by repeated calls; fill in the missing nonlocal line.

knowledge_points.title: Without nonlocal: UnboundLocalError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def counter():
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter

c = make_counter()
c()  # UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value
Assigning to count makes it local to counter, exactly like the global case; nonlocal is the fix.
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the missing nonlocal; predict which snippets raise UnboundLocalError.

knowledge_points.title: Every closure has its own state
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def counter():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter

a = make_counter()
b = make_counter()
a(); a()
print(a(), b())  # 3 1
Unlike a global counter, two counters made by the factory never interfere.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace interleaved calls to several counters; write a factory for a running total.

knowledge_points.title: Changing a captured list needs no nonlocal
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_logger():
    log = []
    def add(msg):
        log.append(msg)
        return log
    return add

add = make_logger()
add("start")
print(add("stop"))  # ['start', 'stop']
nonlocal is needed only to rebind a name (=, +=); calling a method on the object is not rebinding.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which inner functions need nonlocal; predict outputs of closures that mutate a list.

def power(exponent):

square = power(2)
cube = power(3)
print(list(map(cube, [1, 2, 3])))  # [1, 8, 27]

knowledge_points.worked_example:
def volume(length):
    return lambda width: lambda height: length * width * height

print(volume(2)(3)(4))  # 24
base_2x3 = volume(2)(3)
print(base_2x3(10))  # 60

from functools import partial

from_binary = partial(int, base=2)
print(from_binary("101"))  # 5

topics.title: Decorators for any function: *args, **kwargs and functools.wraps
topics.summary: Write a wrapper that accepts and forwards any arguments with *args and **kwargs, and keep the original's name with functools.wraps.

topics.title: Generator functions and yield
topics.summary: Write a generator function with yield, step through it with next() and for, and know that a generator is used up after one pass.

knowledge_points.title: yield turns a function into a generator
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a for loop over a generator prints; write a generator for a described sequence.

knowledge_points.title: Calling it runs nothing yet; next() runs to the next yield
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def count_up(n):
    i = 1
    while i <= n:
        yield i
        i += 1

g = count_up(2)
print(next(g), next(g))  # 1 2
next(g)  # StopIteration
count_up(2) only creates a generator object; next() runs the body until the next yield, and StopIteration means it finished.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict a sequence of next() calls, including the one that raises StopIteration.

knowledge_points.title: yield pauses; return ends
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def steps():
    print("A")
    yield 1
    print("B")
    yield 2
    print("C")

for value in steps():
    print(value)  # A 1 B 2 C, one per line
Local state and position are kept between values; return (or reaching the end) stops the generator for good.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace interleaved prints from a generator and its loop; contrast with a function that returns a list.

knowledge_points.title: A generator is used up after one pass
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def count_up(n):
    i = 1
    while i <= n:
        yield i
        i += 1

g = count_up(3)
print(list(g))  # [1, 2, 3]
print(list(g))  # []
list(g) collects every value; the second pass finds nothing. Call count_up(3) again for a fresh generator.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of reusing a generator; fix code that loops twice over one generator.

topics.title: Lazy and infinite generators
topics.summary: Write generators that produce values only when asked, including endless ones consumed with break, and generators that yield only matching values.

knowledge_points.title: An endless generator and a loop that breaks
knowledge_points.practice: Predict where a loop over an endless generator stops; write the loop that finds the first value passing a test.

knowledge_points.title: Taking the first n values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def naturals():
    n = 1
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 1

g = naturals()
first = []
for _ in range(3):
    first.append(next(g))
print(first)  # [1, 2, 3]
print(next(g))  # 4
next() continues the same generator, so the following call carries on from 4.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values when next() is called on a generator between loops; write a take(g, n) helper.

knowledge_points.title: Yielding only some values
knowledge_points.practice: Write generators that produce primes, evens or matching words; predict their first few values.

knowledge_points.title: return stops a generator early
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of generators with an early return; fix one that uses break where the caller expects it to stop.

topics.title: Generator expressions
topics.summary: Write (expr for x in items) and (expr for x in items if cond) and pass them straight to sum(), max() and similar built-ins.

knowledge_points.title: Parentheses make a generator expression
knowledge_points.worked_example:
squares = (x * x for x in range(5))
print(squares)  # <generator object <genexpr> at 0x...>
print(list(squares))  # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
It is a one-line generator: nothing is computed until something asks for values.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert short generator functions to generator expressions; predict their contents with list().

knowledge_points.title: Drop the brackets of a comprehension inside a call
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
print(max([len(w) for w in words]))  # 6: builds a list first
print(max(len(w) for w in words))    # 6: no list is ever built
print(sum(x * x for x in range(1, 4)))  # 14
Inside a call's own parentheses no extra pair is needed; the values arrive one at a time.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite comprehensions passed to sum(), max() and any() as generator expressions; compare with the equivalent map(); predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Filtering with if
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
print(sum(1 for w in words if len(w) > 3))  # 2
The if keeps only matching items; sum(1 for ...) counts them.
knowledge_points.practice: Count and total items that meet a condition with a single expression.

knowledge_points.title: Used up after one pass, like any generator
knowledge_points.worked_example:
evens = (n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 0)
print(sum(evens))  # 6
print(sum(evens))  # 0
The second sum finds the generator empty; build a list if you need the values twice.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict repeated use of one generator expression; fix code that reuses it.

topics.title: Chaining generators into pipelines
topics.summary: Connect generators so each one consumes another's output, and delegate to another iterable with yield from.

knowledge_points.title: One generator feeding another
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of two- and three-stage pipelines; write a stage for a described step.

knowledge_points.title: yield from hands over to another iterable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def both(a, b):
    yield from a
    yield from b

print(list(both([1, 2], "ab")))  # [1, 2, 'a', 'b']
yield from x is short for: for item in x: yield item.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite for/yield loops with yield from; predict the combined output.

knowledge_points.title: A text-cleaning pipeline
knowledge_points.worked_example:
lines = ["  apple ", "", " pear", "   "]
stripped = (line.strip() for line in lines)
non_empty = (line for line in stripped if line)
print(list(non_empty))  # ['apple', 'pear']
Each stage is one small step; nothing runs until list() pulls values through.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the stages of a pipeline to produce a target result; add a stage that upper-cases.

topics.title: Any number of positional arguments: *args
topics.summary: Define functions with *args, use the tuple it collects, and combine it with ordinary and keyword-only parameters.

knowledge_points.title: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def show(*args):
    print(args)

show(1, 2, 3)  # (1, 2, 3)
show()  # ()
The star in the def means: pack all positional arguments into one tuple; the name args is only a convention.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the tuple collected for different calls, including no arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Looping over args
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def total(*numbers):
    result = 0
    for n in numbers:
        result += n
    return result

print(total(4, 5, 6))  # 15
print(total())  # 0
args is an ordinary tuple: loop over it, index it, take its len.
knowledge_points.practice: Write *args functions such as largest(*nums) or average(*nums); handle the no-argument case.

knowledge_points.title: Ordinary parameters first, then *args
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which arguments land in which parameter; fill in a def line for a described call.

knowledge_points.title: Parameters after *args must be passed by keyword
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of calls with and without the keyword; fix calls that pass the option by position.

topics.title: Any number of keyword arguments: **kwargs
topics.summary: Define functions with **kwargs, read the dict it collects, and order ordinary, *args, keyword-only and **kwargs parameters correctly.

knowledge_points.title: **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict collected for different calls.

knowledge_points.title: Reading the collected values
knowledge_points.practice: Write functions that print or build text from their keyword arguments; look up one expected key.

knowledge_points.title: The full order: normal, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs
knowledge_points.practice: Predict where each argument goes; put the parameters of a def in a legal order.

knowledge_points.title: Positional arguments cannot go into **kwargs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def show(**kwargs):
    print(kwargs)

show("Ana")  # TypeError: show() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given
**kwargs only accepts name=value arguments; add *args if positional ones are needed too.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise TypeError; fix the def or the call.

topics.title: Spreading a list or dict into a call with * and **
topics.summary: Unpack a list or tuple into positional arguments with * and a dict into keyword arguments with **, and forward arguments from one function to another.

knowledge_points.title: * in a call spreads a sequence into arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

size = [3, 4]
print(area(*size))  # 12
Just as print(*nums) spreads a list into print, area(*size) is area(3, 4); without the star, size would be one argument.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict calls that use *; fix a call that passes a list where separate arguments are needed.

knowledge_points.title: The counts must match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

print(area(*[1, 2, 3]))  # TypeError: area() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given
The star spreads every item; the function still decides how many it accepts.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which spread calls succeed; predict the error message for the others.

knowledge_points.title: ** in a call spreads a dict into keyword arguments
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite keyword calls using a dict and **; predict the result.

knowledge_points.title: Forwarding arguments to another function
knowledge_points.practice: Write a forwarding function; predict results of forwarded calls.

topics.title: Keyword-only and positional-only parameters: * and /
topics.summary: Use a bare * to force keyword arguments and / to forbid them, and read these markers in function signatures.

knowledge_points.title: A bare * makes the following parameters keyword-only
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_box(*, width, height):
    return width * height

print(make_box(width=2, height=5))  # 10
make_box(2, 5)  # TypeError: make_box() takes 0 positional arguments but 2 were given
Forcing names stops callers mixing up arguments of the same type.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls succeed; add * to a def so a call must name its options.

knowledge_points.title: / makes the earlier parameters positional-only
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def half(x, /):
    return x / 2

print(half(8))  # 4.0
half(x=8)  # TypeError: half() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'x'
Parameters before / cannot be named in the call, so their names can change freely later.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise TypeError for a def using /.

knowledge_points.title: Reading signatures with / and *
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# sorted(iterable, /, *, key=None, reverse=False)
print(sorted([3, 1, 2], reverse=True))  # [3, 2, 1]
sorted([3, 1, 2], True)  # TypeError: sorted expected 1 argument, got 2
help() shows signatures like this: iterable is positional-only, key and reverse are keyword-only.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a signature, decide which calls are legal; write the def line for a described signature.

topics.title: Recursion: functions that call themselves
topics.summary: Write a recursive function with a base case that stops and a recursive case that moves toward it, for countdowns, sums, factorials and powers.

knowledge_points.title: A function that calls itself
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of short recursive printing functions; identify the base case and the recursive call.

knowledge_points.title: Base case returns, recursive case builds on a smaller call
knowledge_points.practice: Predict return values; fill in the base case or the recursive expression.

knowledge_points.title: Factorial from its definition
knowledge_points.practice: Write factorial and similar product functions; predict results for small inputs.

knowledge_points.title: Writing a function from a recurrence
knowledge_points.practice: Given a rule in words, write the recursive function (power, multiply by adding, count digits).

topics.title: Tracing recursive calls
topics.summary: Trace recursive calls with a call stack: each call's own variables, work done before versus after the recursive call, and how results return.

knowledge_points.title: Each call has its own n
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a trace table of calls and their n values; count how many calls a given input makes.

knowledge_points.title: Results return back up the stack
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the return value of each call in order; predict the final result.

knowledge_points.title: Work before or after the recursive call
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output order for functions that print before, after, or both.

topics.title: Fixing recursion bugs: missing base cases and lost results
topics.summary: Recognise and fix RecursionError from a missing or unreachable base case, None from a missing return, and inputs too deep for recursion.

knowledge_points.title: No base case: RecursionError
knowledge_points.practice: Spot which recursive functions can never stop; add the missing base case.

knowledge_points.title: A base case the input never reaches
knowledge_points.practice: Trace inputs that jump over the base case; fix the condition.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting to return the recursive result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def sum_to(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    n + sum_to(n - 1)  # bug: no return

print(sum_to(1))  # None
print(sum_to(2))  # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'NoneType'
The recursive case computed a value and threw it away, so the call returned None.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a function missing return gives; fix it.

knowledge_points.title: Correct but too deep: use a loop
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which inputs exceed the limit; rewrite a simple recursive function as a loop.

topics.title: Recursion on strings and lists
topics.summary: Solve string and list problems recursively by handling the first item (or both ends) and recursing on the rest via slicing.

knowledge_points.title: First character plus the rest
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of recursive string functions; write count_vowels(s) recursively.

knowledge_points.title: First item plus the rest of a list
knowledge_points.practice: Write recursive length, total and maximum of a list; trace one call chain.

knowledge_points.title: Working from both ends
knowledge_points.practice: Predict palindrome checks; fill in the missing base case.

knowledge_points.title: Building a new list recursively
knowledge_points.practice: Write recursive filters and transforms that return lists; compare with the loop version.

topics.title: Branching recursion: Fibonacci and Towers of Hanoi
topics.summary: Write recursive functions that make two calls per step, trace their call trees, and recognise why naive versions grow exponentially.

knowledge_points.title: Two recursive calls and two base cases
knowledge_points.practice: Predict small Fibonacci values; write a recursive function with two calls (e.g. a 1-or-2-steps staircase count).

knowledge_points.title: The call tree
knowledge_points.practice: Count the calls in a call tree; list the calls in the order they happen.

knowledge_points.title: Why naive branching recursion gets slow
knowledge_points.practice: Estimate how the call count grows as n grows; choose which functions will be slow.

knowledge_points.title: Towers of Hanoi: solving by trusting the smaller call
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def hanoi(n, start, end, spare):
    if n == 0:
        return
    hanoi(n - 1, start, spare, end)
    print("move", n, start, "->", end)
    hanoi(n - 1, spare, end, start)

hanoi(2, "A", "C", "B")  # move 1 A -> B / move 2 A -> C / move 1 B -> C
Move n - 1 disks out of the way, move the biggest, move the n - 1 back on top: assume the smaller call works.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the moves for 2-3 disks; count moves for n disks (2^n - 1).

topics.title: Recursion on nested lists
topics.summary: Process lists that contain lists to any depth (sum, flatten, depth) by recursing whenever an item is itself a list.

knowledge_points.title: Items that are lists themselves
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = [1, [2, 3], [4, [5]]]
for item in data:
    print(item, isinstance(item, list))
# 1 False / [2, 3] True / [4, [5]] True
A loop sees only the top level; isinstance(item, list) tells which items need going into.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() and the type checks of nested lists; count top-level items.

knowledge_points.title: Summing at every depth
knowledge_points.practice: Write nested_sum / nested_count; trace which calls are made for a small input.

knowledge_points.title: Flattening into one list
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a flatten that uses append for sub-lists; predict flatten results.

knowledge_points.title: Measuring the depth
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the depth of given lists; write the function that finds the largest number at any depth.

topics.title: Speeding up recursion: caching and loops
topics.summary: Make branching recursion fast by caching results, with functools.cache or a hand-written dict, or by rewriting it as a loop.

knowledge_points.title: The same subproblems are solved again and again
knowledge_points.practice: Count repeated calls in a call tree; choose which inputs are recomputed.

knowledge_points.title: @cache remembers results
knowledge_points.practice: Add @cache to slow recursive functions; predict how many times the body runs for a given input.

knowledge_points.title: Or count up with a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def fib(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a

print(fib(10))  # 55
Building from the base cases upward needs only the last two values and no recursion at all.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the two-variable loop; rewrite another branching recursion (staircase count) as a loop.

knowledge_points.title: Memoising by hand with a dict
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the lookup and store lines of a memoised function; trace which calls are answered from the dict.

topics.title: Pure functions and side effects
topics.summary: Tell pure functions (same inputs, same output, nothing else changed) from ones with side effects or hidden inputs, and rewrite impure functions as pure ones.

knowledge_points.title: Same inputs, same output, nothing else changes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

print(area(3, 4), area(3, 4))  # 12 12
area is pure: its result depends only on its arguments and calling it changes nothing.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify short functions as pure or not, giving the reason.

knowledge_points.title: Side effects: printing, input, changing globals, mutating arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add_item(cart, item):
    cart.append(item)
    return cart

mine = ["tea"]
add_item(mine, "jam")
print(mine)  # ['tea', 'jam']
The caller's list changed: that is a side effect, even though the function also returns a value.
knowledge_points.practice: Identify every side effect in given functions; predict the state of variables after the calls.

knowledge_points.title: Hidden inputs: reading a global
knowledge_points.worked_example:
rate = 0.2

def with_tax(price):
    return price * (1 + rate)

print(with_tax(10))  # 12.0
rate = 0.5
print(with_tax(10))  # 15.0
Same argument, different result: the global is an input the call does not show.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results after a global changes; fix the function by making the value a parameter.

knowledge_points.title: Rewriting an impure function as a pure one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add_item(cart, item):
    return cart + [item]

mine = ["tea"]
new = add_item(mine, "jam")
print(mine, new)  # ['tea'] ['tea', 'jam']
Return a new value instead of changing the old one; pure functions are easy to test and reuse.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite functions that mutate, print or read globals so they are pure.

topics.title: From loops to map, filter and built-ins: declarative style
topics.summary: Rewrite imperative accumulation loops as compositions of filter, map, sorted and sum, without mutating data, and judge which version reads better.

knowledge_points.title: Same task, two styles
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 8, 1, 6]
total = 0
for n in nums:
    if n > 2:
        total += n * n
print(total)  # 109
print(sum(map(lambda n: n * n, filter(lambda n: n > 2, nums))))  # 109
The loop says how to compute step by step; the second line says what: square the large ones and add.
knowledge_points.practice: Match loops to equivalent map/filter/sum expressions; predict both versions.

knowledge_points.title: Building a pipeline step by step
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["Pear", "fig", "Apple", "kiwi"]
lower = map(str.lower, words)
long = filter(lambda w: len(w) > 3, lower)
print(sorted(long))  # ['apple', 'kiwi', 'pear']
Each step takes the previous result; read the pipeline in order.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps of a pipeline (Parsons); write one for a described transformation.

knowledge_points.title: No mutation: produce new values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 95, 82]
ranked = sorted(scores, reverse=True)
print(scores, ranked)  # [70, 95, 82] [95, 82, 70]
sorted returns a new list and leaves scores alone; sort() would have changed it.
knowledge_points.practice: Replace mutating steps (sort, append, +=) with expressions that return new values.

knowledge_points.title: When the loop reads better
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Hard to read:
# print(list(map(lambda p: p[0], filter(lambda p: p[1] > 50 and p[0] != "x", pairs))))
pairs = [("a", 60), ("x", 90), ("b", 40)]
for name, score in pairs:
    if score > 50 and name != "x":
        print(name)  # a
Deeply nested map/filter with long lambdas is harder to read than a short loop; pick the clearer one.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the clearer version for several tasks and justify the choice.

topics.title: Folding a list into one value with reduce()
topics.summary: Use functools.reduce with and without an initial value, trace how it combines items, and prefer sum/max/join when they exist.

knowledge_points.title: reduce combines items two at a time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from functools import reduce

print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [1, 2, 3, 4]))  # 10
# ((1 + 2) + 3) + 4
The function gets the result so far and the next item, like an accumulator loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the accumulator through each step; predict the result.

knowledge_points.title: An initial value, and the empty-list error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from functools import reduce

print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc * x, [2, 3, 4], 1))  # 24
print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [], 0))  # 0
reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [])  # TypeError: reduce() of empty iterable with no initial value
The third argument is the starting accumulator; it also makes empty input safe.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results with and without an initial value; fix a reduce that crashes on empty input.

knowledge_points.title: Reductions that are not sums
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from functools import reduce

words = ["a", "bb", "ccc"]
print(reduce(lambda acc, w: acc + len(w), words, 0))  # 6
print(reduce(lambda a, b: a if a > b else b, [3, 9, 2]))  # 9
The initial value can be a different type from the items (an int for a list of strings).
knowledge_points.practice: Write reduce calls for product, maximum and total length.

knowledge_points.title: Prefer the built-in when there is one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 9, 2]
print(sum(nums), max(nums), "-".join(["a", "b"]))  # 14 9 a-b
sum, max, min and join are reductions with names; reach for reduce only when none fits.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the clearest tool (built-in, reduce or loop) for described reductions.

topics.title: Reading a traceback
topics.summary: Read a full traceback bottom-up: the error type and message, the failing line, and the chain of calls that led there.

knowledge_points.title: Read the last line first: error type and message
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(10 / 0)
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
The last line names the kind of error (before the colon) and what went wrong (after it).
knowledge_points.practice: Given short tracebacks, name the error type and say in words what went wrong.

knowledge_points.title: Tracebacks through function calls: the bottom frame is where it broke
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def average(total, count):
    return total / count

def report(total, count):
    print(average(total, count))

report(10, 0)
# Traceback lists: line 7 in <module>, line 5 in report, line 2 in average
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
"Most recent call last": read up from the bottom to see who called whom.
knowledge_points.practice: For a three-frame traceback, give the line that raised the error and the order of calls that led there.

knowledge_points.title: The line that fails is not always the line that is wrong
knowledge_points.worked_example:
In the traceback above, line 2 divides correctly; the bad value 0 came from report(10, 0) on line 7.
Follow the frames upward until you reach the line that supplied the bad value.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a traceback and the code, pick the line that should be changed to fix the bug.

knowledge_points.title: Use the hints: 'Did you mean' and the ^^^ markers
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 5
print(totl)
# NameError: name 'totl' is not defined. Did you mean: 'total'?
In Python 3.11+ ~~~ and ^^^ under the code point at the exact part of the line that failed.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix snippets using only the information in the error message, then predict the message for a new typo.

topics.title: Recognising the common error types
topics.summary: Match SyntaxError, IndentationError, NameError, TypeError, ValueError, IndexError, ZeroDivisionError and AttributeError to the kinds of mistake that cause them.

knowledge_points.title: SyntaxError and IndentationError: the code is not valid Python
knowledge_points.worked_example:
if True:
print("x")
# IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 1
These are found before any line runs, so nothing is printed.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which snippets fail before running and fix the missing colon, bracket, quote or indent.

knowledge_points.title: NameError: a misspelled or not-yet-assigned name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(score)
score = 10
# NameError: name 'score' is not defined

knowledge_points.title: TypeError vs ValueError: wrong kind of value vs bad value of the right kind

knowledge_points.title: IndexError, ZeroDivisionError and AttributeError

topics.title: Finding logic errors with print
topics.summary: Spot a logic error (the program runs but gives the wrong answer) and locate it by printing values at checkpoints, including inside a loop.

knowledge_points.title: Logic errors: no message, just a wrong answer
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += i
    return total

print(sum_to(3))   # 3, but 1 + 2 + 3 is 6
No traceback appears, so you must compare the output to what you expected.
