knowledge_points.worked_example:
import shapez
# ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'shapez'
from shapes.area import circle
# ImportError: cannot import name 'circle' from 'shapes.area'
The first means no such module; the second means the module exists but lacks that name.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify import errors and pick the fix: spelling, wrong folder, missing name, or a package that is not installed.

knowledge_points.title: Where Python looks: the script's folder first
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import sys
print(sys.path[0])  # the folder of the file you ran
Python searches that folder, then the standard library, then installed packages. That is why random.py shadows random, and why tests run from the project folder can import its modules.
knowledge_points.practice: Given folder layouts and the file that is run (including a tests/ folder), predict which imports succeed.

topics.title: Random numbers: randint, random and randrange
topics.summary: Generate random whole numbers and floats in a chosen range, use random() for chances, and reason about which results are possible.

knowledge_points.title: randint(a, b) includes both ends
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import random
roll = random.randint(1, 6)
print(1 <= roll <= 6)  # True
Unlike range(1, 6), randint(1, 6) can give 6.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the randint call for dice, coins (0/1) and percentages; spot off-by-one ranges.

knowledge_points.title: Predict the possible values, not the value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = random.randint(1, 3) * 2
print(x)  # 2, 4 or 6, different on each run
Random programs are checked by the set of values they can produce.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose every output a random expression could produce; reject impossible ones.

knowledge_points.title: random() for chances
knowledge_points.practice: Write conditions that happen with a given probability; predict which branch is possible for given values of random().

knowledge_points.title: randrange like range, uniform for floats
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = random.randrange(0, 10, 2)  # one of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
t = random.uniform(1.5, 2.5)   # a float from 1.5 to 2.5
randrange takes range's arguments and also excludes stop.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the function and arguments that produce a described set of values.

topics.title: Random picks from a list: choice, shuffle, sample and choices
topics.summary: Pick one item, shuffle a list in place, and draw several items with or without repeats, avoiding the shuffle-returns-None bug.

knowledge_points.title: choice picks one item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import random
move = random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"])
print(move in ["rock", "paper", "scissors"])  # True
random.choice([])
# IndexError: Cannot choose from an empty sequence
knowledge_points.practice: Write choice calls on lists and strings; predict which calls raise IndexError.

knowledge_points.title: shuffle changes the list and returns None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cards = ["A", "K", "Q"]
hand = random.shuffle(cards)
print(hand)  # None
random.shuffle(cards) reorders cards itself; use cards afterwards.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that store the result of shuffle; predict what is printed.

knowledge_points.title: sample(k) draws k different items
knowledge_points.worked_example:
numbers = random.sample(range(1, 50), 6)  # 6 different lottery numbers
random.sample([1, 2, 3], 5)
# ValueError: Sample larger than population or is negative
knowledge_points.practice: Write a lottery draw; predict which sample calls fail.

knowledge_points.title: choices(k=...) allows repeats
knowledge_points.worked_example:
flips = random.choices("HT", k=5)  # a list like ['H', 'T', 'T', 'H', 'H']
Use choices when the same item may come up again (coin flips, password characters), sample when it may not (lottery, dealing).
knowledge_points.practice: Choose sample or choices for described situations; predict length and possible repeats of the result.

topics.title: Repeatable randomness: seed and testing random code
topics.summary: Make random sequences repeat with seed, avoid reseeding in a loop, and keep random calls out of the functions you test.

knowledge_points.title: The same seed gives the same sequence
knowledge_points.worked_example:
random.seed(42)
a = [random.randint(1, 100), random.randint(1, 100)]
random.seed(42)
b = [random.randint(1, 100), random.randint(1, 100)]
print(a == b)  # True
The numbers are pseudo-random: computed from a starting seed.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether two sequences are equal given seed calls; explain why programs differ between runs without a seed.

knowledge_points.title: Seed once, not inside the loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for _ in range(3):
    random.seed(1)
    print(random.randint(1, 6))
# 2
# 2
# 2
Reseeding restarts the sequence every pass.
knowledge_points.practice: Find why a dice loop repeats the same number; move the seed.

knowledge_points.title: Keep randomness outside the function you test
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def is_hit(roll):
    return roll >= 5

result = is_hit(random.randint(1, 6))
assert is_hit(5) and not is_hit(4)
The random value is passed in, so tests can choose it.
knowledge_points.practice: Refactor a function that calls randint internally so it takes the value as a parameter; write asserts for it.

topics.title: Building small games with random
topics.summary: Combine random with loops and lists to write a guessing game, a computer opponent, a password generator and a card deal.

knowledge_points.title: A guessing game with a random secret
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the transcript for a given secret and guesses; reorder the lines of the game loop.

knowledge_points.title: A computer opponent
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result for each possible computer move; fill in the missing winning condition.

knowledge_points.title: Build a random password
knowledge_points.worked_example:
letters = "abcdefghjkmnpqrstuvwxyz23456789"
password = ""
for _ in range(8):
    password += random.choice(letters)
print(len(password))  # 8
knowledge_points.practice: Write a generator for a given length and alphabet; fix one that picks once and repeats the same character.

knowledge_points.title: Shuffle a deck and deal with pop()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
deck = ["A", "K", "Q", "J", "10"]
random.shuffle(deck)
hand = [deck.pop(), deck.pop()]
print(len(hand), len(deck))  # 2 3
Dealt cards leave the deck, so they cannot be dealt twice.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict deck and hand sizes after dealing; write a deal of n cards to two players.

topics.title: The math module: sqrt, pi, floor and ceil
topics.summary: Use math.sqrt, math.pi, floor, ceil and a few other math functions in formulas, and recognise the math domain error.

knowledge_points.title: sqrt and pi in formulas
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import math
area = math.pi * 3 ** 2
print(round(area, 1))  # 28.3
print(math.sqrt(16))  # 4.0 (always a float)
knowledge_points.practice: Translate geometry formulas (circle area, hypotenuse) into Python with math; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: floor and ceil vs int() and round()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(math.floor(3.7), math.ceil(3.2))   # 3 4
print(math.floor(-3.7), int(-3.7))     # -4 -3
floor always goes down, ceil always up; int() just drops the decimals.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict floor/ceil/int/round for positive and negative numbers; choose ceil for 'how many boxes are needed'.

knowledge_points.title: Impossible inputs raise ValueError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(math.sqrt(-1))
# ValueError: math domain error
Check the value first (if d >= 0) when it might be negative.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls fail; add a guard before a square root.

knowledge_points.title: More tools: factorial, gcd, log10
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(math.factorial(5), math.gcd(12, 18), math.log10(1000))  # 120 6 3.0
help(math) lists the rest.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the math function for a described task; predict results.

topics.title: Comparing floats with isclose, infinity, and the quadratic formula
topics.summary: Compare floats with math.isclose (with abs_tol near zero), start min searches at math.inf, and solve a quadratic safely.

knowledge_points.title: isclose instead of ==
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)               # False
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))   # True
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite float equality checks with isclose; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Near zero, isclose needs abs_tol
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(math.isclose(1e-10, 0))               # False
print(math.isclose(1e-10, 0, abs_tol=1e-9))  # True
The default tolerance is relative, so nothing is 'close' to exactly 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict isclose results against 0; add abs_tol to a failing check.

knowledge_points.title: math.inf as a starting value
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the start value for min/max searches (inf or -inf); predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Solving a quadratic equation
knowledge_points.practice: Write the solver; predict output for equations with two, one and no real roots.

topics.title: Dates and times with datetime
topics.summary: Create dates, get today's date and the current time, read their parts, compare them, and avoid the datetime-module-vs-class mix-up.

knowledge_points.title: Make a date and read its parts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from datetime import date
d = date(2024, 3, 15)
print(d)  # 2024-03-15
print(d.year, d.month, d.day)  # 2024 3 15
print(d.weekday())  # 4 (Monday is 0, so Friday)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict printed dates and parts; write the date for a described day.

knowledge_points.title: Today and now
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from datetime import date, datetime
today = date.today()
now = datetime.now()
print(now.hour, now.minute)  # e.g. 14 5
The values depend on when the program runs.
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that prints today's year or greets by time of day; choose date or datetime for a task.

knowledge_points.title: The module and the class share a name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import datetime
print(datetime.now())
# AttributeError: module 'datetime' has no attribute 'now'
Fix: from datetime import datetime, or datetime.datetime.now().
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that mix up the datetime module and the datetime class; predict which lines fail.

knowledge_points.title: Compare dates; impossible dates fail
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(date(2024, 12, 25) > date(2024, 3, 15))  # True
date(2024, 2, 30)
# ValueError: day is out of range for month
knowledge_points.practice: Predict comparisons between dates; predict which dates can be created.

topics.title: Date arithmetic with timedelta
topics.summary: Subtract dates to get a timedelta, add days or hours to a date or datetime, and convert durations to days or minutes.

knowledge_points.title: date - date gives a timedelta
knowledge_points.practice: Predict days between dates (including negative results); write a days-until-birthday calculation.

knowledge_points.title: date + timedelta crosses months and leap years
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from datetime import date, timedelta
print(date(2024, 1, 31) + timedelta(days=30))  # 2024-03-01
print(date(2024, 3, 1) - timedelta(days=1))   # 2024-02-29
knowledge_points.practice: Predict due dates after adding days; write a 'one week from today' expression.

knowledge_points.title: Hours and minutes with datetime
knowledge_points.worked_example:
start = datetime(2024, 3, 15, 9, 30)
end = start + timedelta(hours=2, minutes=45)
print(end)  # 2024-03-15 12:15:00
print((end - start).total_seconds() / 60)  # 165.0
knowledge_points.practice: Predict end times; convert durations to minutes or hours.

knowledge_points.title: You cannot add a plain number to a date
knowledge_points.worked_example:
date(2024, 3, 15) + 30
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'datetime.date' and 'int'
Wrap the number: timedelta(days=30).
knowledge_points.practice: Fix date arithmetic that uses plain numbers.

topics.title: Formatting and parsing dates
topics.summary: Turn dates into text with strftime and f-string format codes, and turn text into dates with strptime and fromisoformat, handling bad input.

knowledge_points.title: strftime: date to text with % codes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
d = date(2024, 3, 5)
print(d.strftime("%d.%m.%Y"))     # 05.03.2024
print(d.strftime("%A %d %B %Y"))  # Tuesday 05 March 2024
knowledge_points.practice: Predict strftime output; write the format string for a described layout.

knowledge_points.title: The same codes inside an f-string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(f"{d:%Y-%m-%d}")  # 2024-03-05
print(f"Due: {d:%b %d}")  # Due: Mar 05
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite strftime calls as f-strings; predict output.

knowledge_points.title: strptime and fromisoformat: text to date
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from datetime import datetime, date
d = datetime.strptime("15.03.2024", "%d.%m.%Y")
print(d.date())  # 2024-03-15
print(date.fromisoformat("2024-03-15").year)  # 2024
knowledge_points.practice: Write the format string that parses a given text; predict the parsed date.

knowledge_points.title: Text that does not match raises ValueError
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which inputs parse; write the try/except that prints a format hint for bad input.

topics.title: Summary statistics with the statistics module
topics.summary: Compute mean, median, mode and standard deviation of a list, choose median when outliers distort the mean, and handle empty data.

knowledge_points.title: mean, median and mode
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import statistics
scores = [70, 85, 85, 90, 100]
print(statistics.mean(scores), statistics.median(scores), statistics.mode(scores))
# 86 85 85
mean replaces sum(scores) / len(scores).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the three statistics for short lists; rewrite a sum/len average with mean.

knowledge_points.title: Median of an even-length list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(statistics.median([3, 1, 4, 2]))  # 2.5
print(statistics.median([3, 1, 4]))     # 3
median sorts first; with an even count it averages the middle two.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict medians of odd and even lists, unsorted input included.

knowledge_points.title: An outlier pulls the mean, not the median
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pay = [30, 32, 35, 31, 400]
print(statistics.mean(pay), statistics.median(pay))  # 105.6 32
knowledge_points.practice: Choose mean or median to describe given data; predict the effect of adding an outlier.

knowledge_points.title: Spread with stdev; empty data raises an error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(round(statistics.stdev([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]), 2))  # 2.14
statistics.mean([])
# statistics.StatisticsError: mean requires at least one data point
knowledge_points.practice: Compare spreads of two lists; add an empty-list guard before computing statistics.

topics.title: Installing packages with pip
topics.summary: Install, list, upgrade and uninstall packages from PyPI with python -m pip, and tell which modules need installing.

knowledge_points.title: Install a package, then import it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 -c "import prettytable"
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'prettytable'
$ python3 -m pip install prettytable
Successfully installed prettytable-3.x wcwidth-0.x
Now import prettytable works. pip downloads from PyPI, the Python Package Index.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps to install and use a package; choose the command that fixes a ModuleNotFoundError.

knowledge_points.title: python -m pip installs into the Python you run
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ pip install requests       # may go to a different Python
$ python3 -m pip install requests   # goes to the python3 you run
'Installed but still ModuleNotFoundError' usually means two Pythons.
knowledge_points.practice: Diagnose transcripts where a package was installed for a different interpreter; pick the corrected command.

knowledge_points.title: list, show, upgrade, uninstall
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 -m pip list
$ python3 -m pip show prettytable   # version, location, requires
$ python3 -m pip install --upgrade prettytable
$ python3 -m pip uninstall prettytable
knowledge_points.practice: Match commands to tasks; read pip show output to answer which version is installed.

knowledge_points.title: The standard library needs no install
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import math, random, json, csv   # come with Python
import requests, pytest           # must be installed first
'pip install random' is never needed.
knowledge_points.practice: Sort module names into standard library vs needs pip install.

topics.title: Virtual environments with venv
topics.summary: Create, activate, use and deactivate a per-project virtual environment so each project gets its own packages.

knowledge_points.title: Why one environment per project
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Project A needs library v1, project B needs v2; one shared Python can hold only one.
A virtual environment is a folder with its own Python and its own installed packages.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which problems a virtual environment solves (version clashes, clean installs) and which it does not.

knowledge_points.title: Create and activate
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
(.venv) $ python -m pip install prettytable
The (.venv) prefix shows it is active; installs now go into .venv.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the commands to start a new project with a venv; read a prompt to tell whether a venv is active.

knowledge_points.title: Check which Python is active
knowledge_points.worked_example:
(.venv) $ which python
/home/ada/project/.venv/bin/python
(.venv) $ deactivate
$ which python3
/usr/bin/python3
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which interpreter runs, and where a package installs, before and after activate/deactivate.

knowledge_points.title: Do not commit or edit .venv
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Add .venv/ to .gitignore; delete and recreate it rather than editing it.
The environment can be rebuilt from a requirements file.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which project files to share and which to recreate.

topics.title: Recording dependencies in requirements.txt
topics.summary: Write a requirements.txt with pip freeze or by hand, pin versions, and recreate an environment with pip install -r.

knowledge_points.title: pip freeze lists exact versions
knowledge_points.worked_example:
(.venv) $ python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt
$ cat requirements.txt
prettytable==3.10.0
wcwidth==0.2.13
knowledge_points.practice: Read a requirements file: which packages and versions; predict what freeze prints after installs.

knowledge_points.title: Recreate the environment with -r
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps for running someone else's project.

knowledge_points.title: Version specifiers: ==, >=, ~=
knowledge_points.worked_example:
requests==2.32.3   # exactly this version
requests>=2.30     # this or newer
requests~=2.32     # 2.32 or a later 2.x
Only third-party packages go in the file, never math or random.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which versions satisfy a specifier; fix a requirements file that lists standard-library modules.

topics.title: Finding, installing and importing third-party packages
topics.summary: Find a package on PyPI, know that its install name can differ from its import name, diagnose why it will not import, and prefer the standard library when it suffices.

knowledge_points.title: Install name vs import name
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ python3 -m pip install beautifulsoup4   ->  import bs4
$ python3 -m pip install pillow           ->  import PIL
$ python3 -m pip install python-dotenv    ->  import dotenv
The package page on PyPI shows both names.
knowledge_points.practice: Match install commands to import lines; fix an import that uses the install name.

knowledge_points.title: Why a package will not import
knowledge_points.worked_example:
ModuleNotFoundError after installing usually means one of: not installed in this Python or venv, wrong import name, or your own file has the same name.
Check with python -m pip show <name>.
knowledge_points.practice: Diagnose short transcripts and pick the fix.

knowledge_points.title: Standard library first
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Reading JSON: json (built in). Averages: statistics (built in). Web pages over HTTP: requests (third-party) is much simpler than urllib.
Each install is a dependency to keep updated.
knowledge_points.practice: For described tasks, choose a standard-library module or a third-party package.

topics.title: Using a new package from its documentation
topics.summary: Read a package's quickstart, adapt its example code to your own data, and look up options in its reference docs.

knowledge_points.title: Start from the quickstart example
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from prettytable import PrettyTable
table = PrettyTable()
table.field_names = ["Pokemon", "Type"]
table.add_row(["Pikachu", "Electric"])
print(table)   # a boxed text table with a header row
Copy the import line exactly; the object's methods are called with a dot, like string methods.

knowledge_points.title: Adapt the example to your data
knowledge_points.worked_example:
rows = [["Pikachu", "Electric"], ["Squirtle", "Water"]]
for row in rows:
    table.add_row(row)
Keep the docs' structure; swap in your own values and loops.

knowledge_points.title: Look up an option in the reference
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Docs: table.align = 'l' left-aligns every column.
table.align = "l"
help(PrettyTable.add_row) also shows a method's parameters.

topics.title: Searching text with re.search
topics.summary: Search for a pattern with re.search, test the result for None, read the matched text with group(), and write patterns as raw strings.

knowledge_points.title: re.search returns a match or None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import re
print(re.search("cat", "concatenate"))  # <re.Match object; span=(3, 6), match='cat'>
print(re.search("dog", "concatenate"))  # None
if re.search("cat", "my cat"):
    print("found")
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether each search finds a match; use search in an if.

knowledge_points.title: group() gives the matched text; check for None first
knowledge_points.worked_example:
m = re.search("dog", "a cat")
print(m.group())
# AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'group'
Write if m: before m.group().
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that call group() on a failed search; predict the text returned by group().

knowledge_points.title: . matches any character; \. matches a dot
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.search("c.t", "the cut rope").group())  # cut
print(re.search("3.14", "pi is 3x14") is None)    # False
print(re.search(r"3\.14", "pi is 3x14") is None)  # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict matches for patterns containing . and \.; fix a pattern that matches too much.

knowledge_points.title: Write patterns as raw strings
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.search("\bcat\b", "a cat sat"))          # None
print(re.search(r"\bcat\b", "a cat sat").group())  # cat
Without r, Python turns \b into a backspace before re sees it (\b means word edge).
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which patterns need the r prefix; fix patterns broken by escape sequences.

topics.title: Character classes and repetition in patterns
topics.summary: Match sets of characters with [...] and \d \w \s, and control repetition with + * ? and {n,m}.

knowledge_points.title: [...] matches one character from a set
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.search("gr[ae]y", "a grey cat").group())  # grey
print(re.search("[0-9]", "room B12").group())      # 1
print(re.search("[^0-9 ]", "42 x").group())        # x
[a-z] is a range; [^...] means any character not listed.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the first match for set and range patterns; write a set for vowels or hex digits.

knowledge_points.title: Shorthands \d, \w, \s
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.search(r"\d\d", "Room 7, floor 12").group())  # 12
print(re.search(r"\w+", "  hello world").group())    # hello
\d digit, \w letter/digit/underscore, \s whitespace.
knowledge_points.practice: Translate between shorthands and [...] sets; predict matches.

knowledge_points.title: + one or more, * zero or more, ? optional
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.search(r"\d+", "order 4521 shipped").group())  # 4521
print(re.search(r"colou?r", "nice color").group())   # color
print(re.search(r"ab*c", "ac").group(), re.search(r"ab+c", "ac"))  # ac None
knowledge_points.practice: Predict matches for patterns with + * ?; choose the quantifier for a description.

knowledge_points.title: {n} and {n,m} for exact counts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.search(r"\d{3}", "12 345 6789").group())  # 345
print(re.search(r"\d{2,4}", "1 23456").group())    # 2345
Repetition takes as many as allowed (greedy).
knowledge_points.practice: Write patterns for a 5-digit ZIP or a 2-4 letter code; predict matches.

topics.title: Validating input with anchors and fullmatch
topics.summary: Anchor patterns with ^ and $, check whole strings with re.fullmatch, write is_valid_...() functions with regex, and ignore case with a flag.

knowledge_points.title: search finds a part; ^ and $ pin the ends
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(re.search(r"\d{5}", "zip 920371")))   # True
print(bool(re.search(r"^\d{5}$", "920371")))      # False
print(bool(re.search(r"^\d{5}$", "92037")))       # True
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which strings pass anchored and unanchored patterns; fix a validator that accepts extra characters.

knowledge_points.title: re.fullmatch checks the whole string
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{5}", "92037")), bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{5}", "920371")))  # True False
fullmatch is the same as anchoring both ends.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite anchored searches as fullmatch; predict results.

knowledge_points.title: A validator function with fullmatch
knowledge_points.practice: Write is_valid_...() for PINs, times (9:00) and codes; replace a hand-written isdigit/len check with a pattern.

knowledge_points.title: re.IGNORECASE
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"yes|y", "YES")))                  # False
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"yes|y", "YES", re.IGNORECASE)))   # True
knowledge_points.practice: Add the flag to make a check case-insensitive; predict results with and without it.

topics.title: Capturing parts with groups and choosing with |
topics.summary: Capture parts of a match with (...) and group(n), choose between alternatives with |, and make parts optional with (...)?.

knowledge_points.title: Parentheses capture parts
knowledge_points.worked_example:
m = re.search(r"(\w+)@(\w+)\.edu", "mail ada@salk.edu now")
print(m.group(), m.group(1), m.group(2))  # ada@salk.edu ada salk
print(m.groups())  # ('ada', 'salk')
knowledge_points.practice: Predict group(n) values; add parentheses to capture a requested part.

knowledge_points.title: Use groups to reorganise text
knowledge_points.practice: Write code that reformats names, dates or times using captured groups.

knowledge_points.title: | means 'or', and needs a group
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(re.search(r"^cat|dog$", "catfish")))    # True: ^cat OR dog$
print(bool(re.search(r"^(cat|dog)$", "catfish")))  # False
| splits the whole pattern unless it is inside parentheses.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of alternations with and without grouping; fix an alternation that accepts too much.

knowledge_points.title: Optional parts with (...)?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
pattern = r"(https?://)?(www\.)?twitter\.com/(\w+)"
print(re.search(pattern, "https://twitter.com/davidjmalan").group(3))  # davidjmalan
print(re.search(pattern, "twitter.com/ada").group(1))  # None
knowledge_points.practice: Predict group values when optional parts are missing; write a pattern that accepts several URL forms.

topics.title: Extracting and replacing: findall, sub and split
topics.summary: Pull every match out of text with findall, search each line of a file, and clean or split text with re.sub and re.split.

knowledge_points.title: findall returns every match as a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.findall(r"\d+", "3 apples, 12 pears, 7 figs"))  # ['3', '12', '7']
print(re.findall(r"x", "abc"))  # []
total = 0
for n in re.findall(r"\d+", "3 apples, 12 pears"):
    total += int(n)
print(total)  # 15
knowledge_points.practice: Predict findall lists; total or count extracted numbers.

knowledge_points.title: With groups, findall returns the groups
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.findall(r"(\w+)=(\d+)", "a=1, b=22"))  # [('a', '1'), ('b', '22')]
One group gives a list of strings; several give a list of tuples.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict findall output with zero, one and two groups; index into the returned tuples.

knowledge_points.title: Search each line of a file
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("mbox.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        m = re.search(r"^From: (\S+@\S+)", line)
        if m:
            print(m.group(1))
# ada@salk.edu
# bo@mit.edu
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop that extracts a field from matching lines; predict output for a short file.

knowledge_points.title: re.sub replaces, re.split splits on a pattern
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too    many   spaces"))  # too many spaces
print(re.split(r"\s*[,;]\s*", "a, b;c ;d"))  # ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
Unlike str.replace and str.split, these take patterns.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict sub/split results; clean messy input (repeated spaces, mixed separators).

topics.title: Regex pitfalls: greedy matching, escaping and match vs search
topics.summary: Use non-greedy quantifiers, escape special characters with re.escape, know that re.match only looks at the start, and test patterns on edge cases.

knowledge_points.title: Greedy .+ vs non-greedy .+?
knowledge_points.worked_example: print(re.search(r"<.+>", "bold").group()) # bold print(re.search(r"<.+?>", "bold").group()) # Adding ? makes the repetition stop as early as possible.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict greedy and non-greedy matches; fix an extraction that grabs too much.

knowledge_points.title: Escape special characters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.search("a.c", "a+c a.c").group())  # a+c
print(re.escape("1+1=2"))  # 1\+1=2
. + * ? ( ) [ ] { } ^ $ | \ are special; escape them with \ or re.escape for user text.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot unescaped special characters; fix patterns that search for literal prices or file names.

knowledge_points.title: re.match only checks the start
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(re.match(r"\d+", "abc 123"))           # None
print(re.match(r"\d+", "123 abc").group())   # 123
match anchors at the start only; fullmatch anchors both ends; search looks anywhere.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of match, search and fullmatch on the same inputs.

knowledge_points.title: Test a pattern on inputs it should reject
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r".+@.+", "a@b@c")))         # True: too loose
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\w+@\w+\.edu", "a@b@c")))  # False
List good and bad inputs and check both.
knowledge_points.practice: For a given validator, pick inputs it wrongly accepts or rejects and tighten the pattern.

topics.title: Reading environment variables with os.environ
topics.summary: Read settings from the environment with os.environ and get() defaults, convert their string values, set them in the terminal, and understand PATH.

knowledge_points.title: os.environ works like a dict
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import os
print(os.environ["HOME"])  # /home/ada
print(os.environ["NO_SUCH_VAR"])
# KeyError: 'NO_SUCH_VAR'
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lookups for present and missing variables.

knowledge_points.title: get() with a default; values are strings
knowledge_points.worked_example:
port = os.environ.get("PORT", "5000")
print(port + 1)
# TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
port = int(os.environ.get("PORT", "5000"))
os.getenv("NAME") is the same as os.environ.get("NAME").
knowledge_points.practice: Write lookups with defaults; fix code that uses a numeric setting without int().

knowledge_points.title: Set a variable in the terminal
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ export GREETING=hello        # Windows PowerShell: $env:GREETING="hello"
$ python3 app.py               # os.environ["GREETING"] is 'hello'
$ GREETING=hi python3 app.py   # only for this one run
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a program prints after a sequence of export and run commands.

knowledge_points.title: PATH tells the shell where programs live
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
'command not found' means no folder on PATH holds that program.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which commands will be found for a given PATH; explain a 'command not found' error.

topics.title: Keeping API keys and secrets out of code
topics.summary: Move secrets from source code into environment variables or a .env file, stop with a clear message when one is missing, and keep .env out of version control.

knowledge_points.title: A key in the code is a leaked key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
API_KEY = "sk-12345"            # bad: anyone who sees the code has it
API_KEY = os.environ.get("WEATHER_API_KEY")   # good: the key lives outside the code
knowledge_points.practice: Fix programs that hard-code keys or passwords; choose which values belong in the environment.

knowledge_points.title: Stop early when a secret is missing
knowledge_points.worked_example:
key = os.environ.get("WEATHER_API_KEY")
if key is None:
    sys.exit("Set WEATHER_API_KEY first")
A clear message now beats a confusing error later.
knowledge_points.practice: Add a missing-variable check to a program; predict what happens with and without the variable.

knowledge_points.title: A .env file with python-dotenv
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# .env
WEATHER_API_KEY=sk-12345
# app.py  (python3 -m pip install python-dotenv)
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
key = os.getenv("WEATHER_API_KEY")
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps to use a .env file; predict the value read for a given .env.

knowledge_points.title: Keep .env out of git; share .env.example
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# .gitignore
.env
# .env.example (committed)
WEATHER_API_KEY=your-key-here
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which files to commit; spot a repository that leaks a secret.

topics.title: Running other programs with subprocess.run
topics.summary: Run a command from Python with subprocess.run, capture its output as text, check its exit code, and stop it with a timeout.

knowledge_points.title: Run a command given as a list
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import subprocess
result = subprocess.run(["python3", "child.py"])
# hi from child
print(result.returncode)  # 0
subprocess.run("python3 child.py")
# FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'python3 child.py'
knowledge_points.practice: Write the argument list for a command line; fix calls that pass one string.

knowledge_points.title: capture_output and text
knowledge_points.worked_example:
r = subprocess.run(["python3", "child.py"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.stdout == "hi from child\n")  # True
Without text=True, r.stdout is bytes: b'hi from child\n'.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict stdout values with and without text=True; compare captured output with an expected string.

knowledge_points.title: Exit codes, stderr and check=True
knowledge_points.worked_example:
r = subprocess.run(["python3", "fail.py"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.returncode, r.stderr.strip())  # 3 oops
subprocess.run(["python3", "fail.py"], check=True)
# subprocess.CalledProcessError: ... returned non-zero exit status 3.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict returncode and whether check=True raises; write code that reports a failed command.

knowledge_points.title: timeout, and never shell=True with user input
knowledge_points.practice: Add a timeout and handler to a call; choose the safe way to pass a user-supplied file name.

topics.title: Working in Jupyter and Colab notebooks
topics.summary: Run code cells, read what a cell displays, predict state when cells run out of order, and restart-and-run-all to check a notebook.

knowledge_points.title: Cells run one at a time and share variables
knowledge_points.worked_example:
[1]: price = 10
[2]: price * 2
     20
The number in brackets is the run order; later cells see variables from earlier runs.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a cell shows given previously run cells.

knowledge_points.title: Only the last expression is displayed
knowledge_points.worked_example:
[3]: price + 1
     price + 2
     12
Like the REPL, a cell echoes its last expression; use print() to show more.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the displayed output of multi-line cells; add print where several values are needed.

knowledge_points.title: Run order, not page order, decides the state
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Cell A: x = 1   Cell B: x = x + 1   Cell C: print(x)
Run A, B, B, C -> 3. Reading top to bottom suggests 2.
Hidden state from out-of-order runs is the classic notebook bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace variable values for a given run order of cells.

knowledge_points.title: Restart and run all; installing in a notebook
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Kernel > Restart & Run All runs every cell top to bottom from a clean state.
%pip install prettytable   (Colab also accepts !pip install)
knowledge_points.practice: Choose when to restart; predict which cells fail after restart-and-run-all in a notebook that relied on deleted cells.

topics.title: Guess and check: trying every possible answer
topics.summary: Solve a problem by looping over every candidate answer and testing each, stopping at the answer, reporting when there is none, and handling negative inputs and two unknowns.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over the candidates, test each one
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a guess-and-check loop prints; fill in the test that checks a guess (e.g. 'guess * guess == x', 'guess * 7 == n').

knowledge_points.title: Stop once the guess is big enough, then check for an exact hit
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output for perfect and non-perfect inputs; write a loop that finds the integer square root of n or reports that there is none.

knowledge_points.title: Negative inputs: search with abs(x), then fix the sign
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = -8
guess = 0
while guess ** 3 < abs(x):
    guess += 1
if x < 0:
    guess = -guess
print(guess)  # -2
With guess ** 3 < x the loop would stop at once for x = -8 (0 < -8 is False) and report 0.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot why the cube-root search gives 0 for negative x and fix it; predict results for -27 and 64.

knowledge_points.title: Two unknowns: one loop inside another
knowledge_points.practice: Write a search for two unknowns (chickens and pigs from heads and legs; coins adding to an amount); count how many pairs a nested search checks.

topics.title: Approximate answers: small steps and a tolerance
topics.summary: Find an approximate square root by stepping a float guess until it is within epsilon of the answer, count the guesses, and stop safely when the step jumps past the answer.

knowledge_points.title: Close enough: abs(guess ** 2 - x) < epsilon
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 2
epsilon = 0.01
print(abs(1.41 ** 2 - x) < epsilon)   # False: 1.9881 is 0.0119 away
print(abs(1.414 ** 2 - x) < epsilon)  # True: 1.999396 is close enough
Most square roots are not exact floats, so we accept any guess whose square is within epsilon of x.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide whether given guesses are good enough for a given epsilon; fill in the tolerance test.

knowledge_points.title: Step the guess up until it is close enough
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
epsilon = 0.01
step = 0.0001
guess = 0.0
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon:
    guess += step
print(round(guess, 4))  # 4.999
The loop runs while the guess is NOT good enough; the condition is the opposite of the 'close enough' test.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of an approximation loop; predict roughly where a loop with a given step stops.

knowledge_points.title: Count the guesses: smaller steps cost more
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
epsilon = 0.01
step = 0.0001
guess = 0.0
num_guesses = 0
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon:
    guess += step
    num_guesses += 1
print(num_guesses)  # 49990
About 5 / 0.0001 guesses. Ten times smaller steps mean ten times more guesses: accuracy costs time.
knowledge_points.practice: Estimate the number of guesses for a given x and step; choose which change (smaller step, larger epsilon) makes the loop faster.

knowledge_points.title: Stepping past the answer: stop when guess ** 2 passes x
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 54321
epsilon = 0.01
step = 0.0001
guess = 0.0
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon and guess ** 2 <= x:
    guess += step
if abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon:
    print('Failed on', x)  # Failed on 54321
else:
    print(guess)
Near 233 each step changes guess ** 2 by about 0.047, more than 2 * epsilon, so it can jump over the window. Without the second condition the loop would never end.
knowledge_points.practice: Find why an approximation loop never ends and add the missing stop condition; predict whether it succeeds for given x, step and epsilon.

topics.title: When float errors pile up
topics.summary: Predict how tiny float errors grow in loops and with large numbers, and avoid them by stopping loops with < and counting with integers (cents, not dollars).

knowledge_points.title: Adding 0.1 ten times is not 1.0
knowledge_points.worked_example:
total = 0.0
for i in range(10):
    total += 0.1
print(total)         # 0.9999999999999999
print(total == 1.0)  # False
Each 0.1 is slightly off, and every addition carries the error along.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result and the == comparison after repeated float additions; rewrite the check with a tolerance.

knowledge_points.title: A float loop runs one time too many
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 0.0
count = 0
while x < 1.0:
    x += 0.1
    count += 1
print(count)  # 11, not 10
After ten steps x is 0.9999999999999999, still < 1.0. With while x != 1.0 the loop would never stop at all.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many times float-stepping loops run; pick which loop condition never terminates.

knowledge_points.title: Count with integers, compute floats from them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cents = 0
for i in range(10):
    cents += 10
print(cents == 100)  # True
print(cents / 100)   # 1.0
Integers are exact. Keep money in cents (or loop over an int i and compute i / 10) and convert only for display.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite a float-stepping loop to use an integer counter; convert a price calculation to cents.

knowledge_points.title: Large plus small: floats keep only about 16 digits
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(1e16 + 1 == 1e16)  # True: the 1 is lost
print(2 ** 60 + 1)       # 1152921504606846977: ints are exact
print(1e308 * 10)        # inf
A float stores about 15-17 significant digits and has a maximum size; Python ints have neither limit.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which expressions lose digits or overflow to inf; choose int or float for counting large quantities exactly.

topics.title: Binary numbers: place values and Python's 0b
topics.summary: Convert between binary and decimal by place value and with 0b literals, bin() and int(s, 2), and work out how many values n bits can hold.

knowledge_points.title: Place values are powers of 2
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# 1011 in binary = 1*8 + 0*4 + 1*2 + 1*1
print(1 * 2**3 + 0 * 2**2 + 1 * 2**1 + 1 * 2**0)  # 11
Like decimal digits are worth 1, 10, 100, binary digits (bits) are worth 1, 2, 4, 8 from the right.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert 4-6 bit binary numbers to decimal by hand; convert small decimals to binary by subtracting powers of 2.

knowledge_points.title: Binary in Python: 0b, bin() and int(s, 2)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(0b1011)          # 11
print(bin(11))         # 0b1011
print(int('1011', 2))  # 11
0b marks a binary literal; bin() returns a string; int() with base 2 reads a binary string.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of bin() and int(..., 2) calls; write the expression that converts a binary string to a number.

knowledge_points.title: n bits give 2 ** n values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(2 ** 8)     # 256: one byte holds 0 to 255
print(bin(255))   # 0b11111111
print(bin(256))   # 0b100000000
Each extra bit doubles the number of values; the largest n-bit number is 2 ** n - 1.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute how many values n bits hold and how many bits a number needs; pick the largest value of a byte.

knowledge_points.title: Hexadecimal: four bits per digit
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(0xff)            # 255
print(hex(255))        # 0xff
print(int('1f', 16))   # 31
Hex digits run 0-9 then a-f (10-15); each hex digit is exactly four bits, which is why colours and bytes are written in hex.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert between short hex, binary and decimal values; predict hex() output.

topics.title: Converting to binary with % 2 and // 2
topics.summary: Write the loop that converts a non-negative or negative integer to a binary string by repeatedly taking n % 2 and n // 2, including the zero case.

knowledge_points.title: The last bit is n % 2, the rest is n // 2
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 11
print(n % 2, n // 2)  # 1 5
# 11 is 0b1011: last bit 1, and 5 is 0b101, the bits that are left
Like n % 10 and n // 10 split off the last decimal digit, % 2 and // 2 split off the last bit.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict n % 2 and n // 2 for several n and match them to the binary digits.

knowledge_points.title: Repeat until n is 0, putting each bit in front
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 11
result = ''
while n > 0:
    result = str(n % 2) + result
    n = n // 2
print(result)  # 1011
Bits come out last-first, so each new bit is added to the front of the string.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace result and n through the loop; reorder the lines of the conversion loop.

knowledge_points.title: Zero needs its own case
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 0
result = ''
while n > 0:
    result = str(n % 2) + result
    n = n // 2
if result == '':
    result = '0'
print(result)  # 0
For n = 0 the loop never runs and result stays empty, so it is fixed up afterwards.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the input that makes the converter print nothing and fix it.

knowledge_points.title: Negative numbers: convert abs(n), then add '-'
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = -6
m = abs(n)
result = ''
while m > 0:
    result = str(m % 2) + result
    m = m // 2
if n < 0:
    result = '-' + result
print(result, bin(n))  # -110 -0b110
Same trick as the negative cube root: work on the size, restore the sign at the end. bin() confirms the answer.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a full to_binary(n) function and check it against bin() for several inputs.

topics.title: Bitwise operators: & | ^ << >>
topics.summary: Combine integers bit by bit with &, | and ^, shift bits with << and >>, and use bit masks as on/off flags without the precedence trap.

knowledge_points.title: & and | work bit by bit
knowledge_points.worked_example:
a, b = 0b1100, 0b1010
print(bin(a & b))  # 0b1000: 1 only where both are 1
print(bin(a | b))  # 0b1110: 1 where either is 1
& and | apply 'and' and 'or' to each pair of bits, unlike the logical and/or which work on whole values.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute & and | of short binary numbers by hand; predict the printed results.

knowledge_points.title: ^ is exclusive or, not a power
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(2 ^ 3)                 # 1: 10 xor 11 = 01
print(2 ** 3)                # 8
print(bin(0b1100 ^ 0b1010))  # 0b110
^ gives 1 where the bits differ. Writing 2 ^ 3 for 'two cubed' is a classic silent bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that uses ^ for powers; predict ^ results.

knowledge_points.title: Shifts multiply and divide by powers of 2
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(5 << 1, 5 << 3)  # 10 40
print(40 >> 2)         # 10
print(bin(5), bin(5 << 1))  # 0b101 0b1010
<< k appends k zero bits (times 2 ** k); >> k drops k bits (floor division by 2 ** k).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict shifted values; write a shift equal to multiplying by 16.

knowledge_points.title: Flags and masks: & is not and
knowledge_points.worked_example:
READ, WRITE, EXEC = 4, 2, 1
perms = READ | WRITE         # 6 = 0b110
print(perms & WRITE != 0)    # True: the write bit is on
print(perms & EXEC != 0)     # False
print(bool(perms and EXEC))  # True: 'and' only asks whether both are non-zero
| switches flags on and & tests one bit. In Python & binds tighter than !=, so no brackets are needed; using the logical and instead of & is the common bug.
knowledge_points.practice: Combine and test permission flags; fix a flag test that uses and instead of &.

topics.title: Why 0.1 cannot be stored exactly
topics.summary: Write fractions in binary, test whether a decimal has an exact binary form by doubling, and see the value Python really stores for 0.1.

knowledge_points.title: Binary fractions: halves, quarters, eighths
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# 0.101 in binary = 1/2 + 0/4 + 1/8
print(1/2 + 1/8)              # 0.625
print(0.625 + 0.125 == 0.75)  # True: both are exact in binary
After the binary point the places are worth 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... Sums of these are stored exactly.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert short binary fractions to decimal; predict which float comparisons are exactly True.

knowledge_points.title: Double until whole: is the fraction exact in binary?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 0.375
p = 0
while x != int(x):
    x = x * 2
    p += 1
print(x, p)  # 3.0 3
0.375 * 2 ** 3 = 3, so 0.375 = 3 / 8 = 0b11 shifted three places: 0.011 in binary.
knowledge_points.practice: Find p for given fractions (0.5, 0.75, 0.6875); write the binary digits from the result.

knowledge_points.title: 1/10 repeats forever in binary
knowledge_points.worked_example:
num, den = 1, 10
bits = ''
for i in range(12):
    num = num * 2
    bits = bits + str(num // den)
    num = num % den
print('0.' + bits)  # 0.000110011001
Long division by 10 in base 2 never ends: 0011 repeats, like 1/3 = 0.333... in decimal. Python must cut it off.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the first binary digits of 1/4 and 1/5 with this loop; classify decimals as exact or repeating in binary.

knowledge_points.title: See the value that is really stored
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(f'{0.1:.20f}')  # 0.10000000000000000555
print(f'{0.5:.20f}')  # 0.50000000000000000000
print(0.1) shows the shortest text that maps back to the stored float; 20 decimals reveal the rounding.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether 20-decimal formatting shows extra digits for given numbers.

topics.title: Exact arithmetic with Decimal and Fraction
topics.summary: Use decimal.Decimal (built from strings) for exact money arithmetic and rounding with quantize, and fractions.Fraction for exact ratios.

knowledge_points.title: Decimal from a string is exact
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2'))                    # 0.3
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2') == Decimal('0.3'))  # True
Decimal stores decimal digits, so 0.1 really is 0.1 and == works without math.isclose. from decimal import Decimal is used as a set phrase here.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict Decimal sums and comparisons next to the same float expressions. Choose between math.isclose (approximate floats) and Decimal (exact decimal values) for described tasks.

knowledge_points.title: Decimal(0.1) copies the float's error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal(0.1))
# 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
The float is already wrong before Decimal sees it. Build Decimals from strings, never from float literals.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix code that builds Decimals from floats; choose the correct constructor call.

knowledge_points.title: Rounding money with quantize
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from decimal import Decimal
print(round(2.675, 2))                            # 2.67: the float is just below 2.675
print(Decimal('2.675').quantize(Decimal('0.01')))  # 2.68
quantize rounds to the given number of places on the exact decimal value (ties go to the even digit by default).
knowledge_points.practice: Round prices to cents with quantize; predict where float round() and quantize disagree.

knowledge_points.title: Fraction for exact ratios
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from fractions import Fraction
print(Fraction(1, 3) + Fraction(1, 6))         # 1/2
print(Fraction(1, 10) * 3 == Fraction(3, 10))  # True
A Fraction keeps an integer numerator and denominator, so thirds and tenths stay exact.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict Fraction results; choose between float, Decimal and Fraction for a task.

topics.title: Bisection: halving the range of possible answers
topics.summary: Approximate a square or cube root by repeatedly guessing the middle of [low, high] and keeping the half that contains the answer, and see why it needs far fewer guesses than stepping.

knowledge_points.title: One bisection step: guess the middle, keep one half
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
low, high = 0.0, x
guess = (low + high) / 2   # 12.5
if guess ** 2 > x:
    high = guess           # the root is in [0, 12.5]
else:
    low = guess
print(low, high)  # 0.0 12.5
If the guess is too big, the answer is below it: move high down. Otherwise move low up.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace low, high and guess for three bisection steps by hand.

knowledge_points.title: Loop until the guess is within epsilon
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
epsilon = 0.01
low, high = 0.0, x
guess = (low + high) / 2
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon:
    if guess ** 2 < x:
        low = guess
    else:
        high = guess
    guess = (low + high) / 2
print(guess)  # 5.00030517578125
Same stopping test as the stepping search; only the way the next guess is chosen has changed.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of the bisection loop; fill in the update of low or high.

knowledge_points.title: Count guesses: halving beats stepping
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
epsilon = 0.01
low, high = 0.0, x
guess = (low + high) / 2
num_guesses = 0
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon:
    if guess ** 2 < x:
        low = guess
    else:
        high = guess
    guess = (low + high) / 2
    num_guesses += 1
print(num_guesses)  # 13 (stepping by 0.0001 took 49990)
Each guess halves the range, so k guesses shrink it by 2 ** k: doubling x adds only about one guess.
knowledge_points.practice: Estimate how many halvings shrink a range below a given width; compare guess counts with the stepping method.

knowledge_points.title: Same method, different function: cube roots
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 27
epsilon = 0.01
low, high = 0.0, x
guess = (low + high) / 2
while abs(guess ** 3 - x) >= epsilon:
    if guess ** 3 < x:
        low = guess
    else:
        high = guess
    guess = (low + high) / 2
print(round(guess, 3))  # 3.0
Bisection only needs to know whether a guess is too big or too small, so it works for any steadily increasing function.
knowledge_points.practice: Adapt the loop to cube roots or to solving guess * guess * 2 == x.

topics.title: Making bisection work for every input
topics.summary: Choose a starting range that really contains the answer (inputs below 1, negative cube roots), package bisection as a function, and guard against an epsilon that floats cannot reach.

knowledge_points.title: Inputs below 1: the root is bigger than x
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 0.25
print(0.5 > x)              # True: sqrt(0.25) = 0.5 is outside [0, x]
low, high = 0.0, max(1.0, x)
print(low, high)            # 0.0 1.0
With high = x every guess is too small, low creeps up to 0.25 and the loop never ends.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether [0, x] contains the root for given x; fix the starting range.

knowledge_points.title: Negative cube roots: the range must include x
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = -27
low, high = min(x, -1.0), max(x, 1.0)
print(low, high)  # -27 1.0
The cube root of -27 is -3, below 0. min and max give a range that works for any sign and size.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose low and high for given x values; predict them from min/max expressions.

knowledge_points.title: Wrap it in a function with a default epsilon
knowledge_points.practice: Write sqrt_bisect(x, epsilon=0.01); predict the results of calls with and without epsilon.

knowledge_points.title: An epsilon floats cannot reach: limit the steps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x, epsilon = 2.0, 1e-20
low, high = 0.0, x
guess = (low + high) / 2
steps = 0
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon and steps < 100:
    if guess ** 2 < x:
        low = guess
    else:
        high = guess
    guess = (low + high) / 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)  # 100: no float is that close to the root of 2
Floats have about 16 digits, so after ~55 halvings low and high stop changing. A step limit turns an endless loop into a clear failure.
knowledge_points.practice: Explain why a given epsilon never ends the loop; add a step limit to a loop.

topics.title: Newton-Raphson: improving a guess with the slope
topics.summary: Apply the Newton-Raphson update guess - f(guess) / f'(guess) to approximate square and cube roots, compare its speed with bisection, and avoid a zero slope.

knowledge_points.title: One Newton step for a square root
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
guess = x / 2   # 12.5
guess = guess - (guess ** 2 - x) / (2 * guess)
print(guess)    # 7.25
For f(g) = g ** 2 - x the slope is 2 * g; following the slope down to zero gives a much better guess.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute one or two Newton steps by hand for given x and starting guesses.

knowledge_points.title: Repeat until close enough
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
epsilon = 0.01
guess = x / 2
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon:
    guess = guess - (guess ** 2 - x) / (2 * guess)
print(guess)  # 5.000012953048684
The loop is the same shape as bisection, but there is no low and high: each guess is computed from the last one.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of the Newton loop; trace the guesses for x = 16.

knowledge_points.title: Count the steps: Newton vs bisection
knowledge_points.worked_example:
x = 25
epsilon = 0.01
guess = x / 2
steps = 0
while abs(guess ** 2 - x) >= epsilon:
    guess = guess - (guess ** 2 - x) / (2 * guess)
    steps += 1
print(steps)  # 4 (bisection needed 13)
Near the answer each Newton step roughly doubles the number of correct digits.
knowledge_points.practice: Count steps for both methods on the same input; choose the faster method for a given situation.

knowledge_points.title: Other functions, and the zero-slope trap
knowledge_points.worked_example:
guess = 1.0
for i in range(8):
    guess = guess - (guess ** 3 - 27) / (3 * guess ** 2)
print(round(guess, 4))  # 3.0
# starting from guess = 0.0: ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
For f(g) = g ** 3 - 27 the slope is 3 * g ** 2 (given). A guess where the slope is 0 cannot be improved.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the Newton update for a given function and slope; fix a loop that starts at 0.

topics.title: Timing code, and why timing is not enough
topics.summary: Measure how long code takes with time.perf_counter, see that timings vary by run and machine, and watch how time grows as the input grows.

knowledge_points.title: Time a piece of code
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import time
start = time.perf_counter()
total = 0
for i in range(1000000):
    total += i
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(round(elapsed, 3), 'seconds')  # e.g. 0.05 seconds
perf_counter() reads a stopwatch; the difference of two readings is the time in between. import time is used as a set phrase.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of a timing snippet; fill in the elapsed-time expression.

knowledge_points.title: Same code, different times
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which factors change a timing (input size, machine, other programs, the code).

knowledge_points.title: Grow the input and watch the time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import time
def total_to(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total += i
    return total
for n in [1000000, 2000000, 4000000]:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    total_to(n)
    print(n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))
# each doubling of n roughly doubles the time
What we care about is the trend: how time changes when the input doubles.
knowledge_points.practice: Given timings for several n, predict the time for a larger n; match timing tables to 'grows like n' or 'stays flat'.

knowledge_points.title: A better algorithm beats a faster computer
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def total_formula(n):
    return n * (n - 1) // 2
print(total_formula(4000000))  # 7999998000000, as fast for n = 4 as for n = 4 million
The formula does one calculation whatever n is; the loop does n additions. As n grows, the gap grows without limit.
knowledge_points.practice: Compare two functions' timing tables and decide which scales better.

topics.title: Counting the steps a program takes
topics.summary: Count the basic steps code performs as a function of the input size n, for single loops, loops in sequence and nested loops, including an inner loop that depends on the outer one.

knowledge_points.title: One step per simple line, n steps for a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def total_to(n):
    total = 0           # 1 step
    for i in range(n):  # n passes
        total += i      # 1 step each pass
    return total        # 1 step
# about n + 2 steps
Counting steps gives the same answer on every machine, unlike timing.
knowledge_points.practice: Count the steps of short functions as an expression in n.

knowledge_points.title: Let the program count for you
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 5
steps = 0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(n):
        steps += 1
print(steps)  # 25 = n * n
Adding a counter to the innermost line checks a step count you worked out by hand.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict a step counter's final value for given n.

knowledge_points.title: Loops one after another add; loops inside loops multiply
knowledge_points.practice: Write the step count in n for code mixing sequential and nested loops.

knowledge_points.title: An inner loop that depends on the outer variable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 10
steps = 0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i):
        steps += 1
print(steps)  # 45 = n * (n - 1) / 2
0 + 1 + ... + (n - 1) steps: about half of n * n, but still growing like n * n.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the count for triangle-shaped loops; choose the formula that matches.

topics.title: Big O: keeping only the fastest-growing term
topics.summary: Describe a step count with Big O by dropping constants and smaller terms, read the order straight from code, and distinguish worst and best case and O from Theta.

knowledge_points.title: Drop constant factors and smaller terms
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for n in [10, 1000]:
    print(n, 3 * n ** 2, 5 * n + 2)
# 10 300 52
# 1000 3000000 5002
For large n the n ** 2 term dwarfs the rest, so 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²): only how fast it grows matters.
knowledge_points.practice: Simplify step-count expressions to Big O (e.g. 4n + 7, n²/2 + n, 100).

knowledge_points.title: Read the order from the code
knowledge_points.practice: Give the Big O of short functions without counting every step.

knowledge_points.title: Worst case and best case
knowledge_points.practice: Name the best- and worst-case inputs for search-like functions and their step counts.

knowledge_points.title: O is an upper bound; Theta is a tight one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
contains() above never takes more than about n steps, so it is O(n).
It is also O(n²) (true but loose). Theta(n) says it grows exactly like n in the worst case.
O(g) means 'grows no faster than g'; Theta(g) means 'grows like g'. When people say O they usually mean the tight bound.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which O and Theta statements about given functions are true.

topics.title: Common growth rates: from O(1) to O(2^n)
topics.summary: Recognise O(log n) halving loops, O(n log n) and exponential branching recursion, and rank the common complexity classes by how fast they grow.

knowledge_points.title: Halving loops are O(log n)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 1000
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)  # 9: about log2(1000)
Each pass halves what is left, so doubling n adds only one step. Bisection works like this.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict step counts of halving loops; identify O(log n) code among several snippets.

knowledge_points.title: A halving loop inside an O(n) loop: O(n log n)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 16
steps = 0
for i in range(n):
    m = n
    while m > 1:
        m = m // 2
        steps += 1
print(steps)  # 64 = 16 * 4
n passes of a log n loop: n log n. Good sorting algorithms land here.
knowledge_points.practice: Count steps and give the class of nested loops mixing halving and counting.

knowledge_points.title: Branching recursion can be exponential
knowledge_points.practice: Predict call counts for small n; classify recursive functions with one vs two recursive calls.

knowledge_points.title: Rank the classes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 30
print(n, n * 5, n ** 2, 2 ** n)  # 30 150 900 1073741824
# roughly: n, n log n, n², 2^n
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n). For big inputs the class matters more than any constant.
knowledge_points.practice: Order functions by growth; pick the largest n each class can handle in a fixed budget.

topics.title: Hidden loops: the cost of in, insert and slicing
topics.summary: Know the Big O of everyday list, set and string operations (in, append, insert(0), slicing) and spot a hidden loop that makes code O(n²).

knowledge_points.title: x in list scans; x in set jumps
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = list(range(1000000))
lookup = set(nums)
print(999999 in nums)    # True, after checking a million items: O(n)
print(999999 in lookup)  # True, found directly: O(1) on average
A list has to be searched item by item; a set (and dict keys) use hashing to go straight to the item.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify membership tests as O(n) or O(1); choose a list or set for frequent lookups.

knowledge_points.title: A hidden loop inside a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def has_duplicates(items):
    seen = []
    for x in items:
        if x in seen:      # scans seen: O(n) each time
            return True
        seen.append(x)
    return False
# O(n²) overall; with seen = set() and seen.add(x) it is O(n)
One line can hide a whole loop. Count the cost of each operation, not just the visible for statements.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the hidden O(n) operation in a loop and rewrite it to bring the whole function down to O(n).

knowledge_points.title: The end of a list is cheap, the front is not
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.append(4)     # O(1): nothing moves
nums.insert(0, 0)  # O(n): every item shifts right
print(nums)        # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
append and pop() work at the end; insert(0, x) and pop(0) shift every item, so they cost O(n).
knowledge_points.practice: Classify list operations by cost; pick the cheaper way to build a list.

knowledge_points.title: Slices copy
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [5, 6, 7, 8]
rest = nums[1:]   # copies 3 items: O(k) for a slice of length k
rest[0] = 99
print(nums)       # [5, 6, 7, 8]: rest is a separate copy
A slice builds a new list, so slicing inside a loop or a recursive call adds a hidden O(n).
knowledge_points.practice: Give the cost of code that slices inside a loop; predict output that shows the copy.

topics.title: Linear search: checking items one by one
topics.summary: Write a linear search that returns the index of the first match or -1, avoid the early-return bug, count its comparisons, and stop early on sorted input.

knowledge_points.title: Return the index of the first match, or -1
knowledge_points.practice: Write linear_search; predict its results for present, absent and repeated targets.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: giving up after the first item
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the misplaced return in search functions.

knowledge_points.title: Count comparisons: linear search is O(n)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = list(range(1000))
checks = 0
for x in nums:
    checks += 1
    if x == 999:
        break
print(checks)  # 1000: the worst case
Best case 1 check, worst case n, about n / 2 on average: O(n). x in nums and nums.index(x) do the same scan.
knowledge_points.practice: Give the number of comparisons for given targets and list sizes.

knowledge_points.title: Sorted input: stop once items pass the target
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how many items are checked; decide whether the early stop changes the Big O.

topics.title: Binary search on a sorted list
topics.summary: Search a sorted list in O(log n) by comparing with the middle item and keeping low/high indexes on the half that can still contain the target.

knowledge_points.title: Look at the middle, throw away half
knowledge_points.worked_example:
items = [3, 8, 12, 19, 25, 31, 40]
low, high = 0, len(items) - 1
mid = (low + high) // 2
print(mid, items[mid])  # 3 19
# looking for 25: 25 > 19, so only indexes 4..6 are left
Bisection on positions: because the list is sorted, one comparison rules out half of it.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace low, mid and high for searches in a 7-15 item list.

knowledge_points.title: The binary search loop
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of binary search; fill in the updates of low and high.

knowledge_points.title: Not found: the range becomes empty
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# binary_search(items, 20) on the list above:
# low=0 high=6 mid=3: 19 < 20, low=4
# low=4 high=6 mid=5: 31 > 20, high=4
# low=4 high=4 mid=4: 25 > 20, high=3
# low=4 > high=3: loop ends, return -1
When low passes high there is nowhere left to look.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace unsuccessful searches to the point where the loop stops; predict the return value.

knowledge_points.title: Only on sorted lists, and why it is O(log n)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(binary_search([40, 3, 25, 8], 8))  # -1, although 8 is there
# a sorted list of 1,000,000 items needs at most 20 comparisons
On unsorted data the halves cannot be ruled out. On sorted data each step halves the range: O(log n) versus O(n) for linear search.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide when binary search can be used; compute the maximum number of comparisons for given sizes.

topics.title: Binary search bugs: off-by-one and endless loops
topics.summary: Find and fix the classic binary search mistakes (< instead of <=, high = len(items), low = mid) and adapt the loop to find the first of several equal items.

knowledge_points.title: while low < high misses the last candidate
knowledge_points.worked_example:
items = [7]
low, high = 0, len(items) - 1
print(low < high, low <= high)  # False True
# with while low < high the loop never runs, so 7 is reported missing
When low == high one item is still left to check, so the condition must be <=.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of a binary search with < for one- and two-item lists; fix the condition.

knowledge_points.title: high = len(items) runs off the end
knowledge_points.worked_example:
items = [3, 8, 12]
low, high = 3, len(items)   # searching for 20: low has moved past 8 and 12
mid = (low + high) // 2
print(items[mid])  # IndexError: list index out of range
high = len(items) is one past the last index. It must be the last valid index, len(items) - 1, when the loop uses <=.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the input that makes a buggy search crash and fix the starting value.

knowledge_points.title: low = mid can loop forever
knowledge_points.worked_example:
low, high = 0, 1
mid = (low + high) // 2   # 0
low = mid                 # still 0
print(low, high)          # 0 1: the next pass picks the same mid
If the range does not shrink on every pass, the loop never ends. Exclude mid with mid + 1 and mid - 1.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace a buggy search until it repeats; fix the update.

knowledge_points.title: Finding the first of several equal items
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what plain and first-match searches return on lists with duplicates; modify the loop to find the last match.

topics.title: Recursive binary search and the bisect module
topics.summary: Write binary search recursively, first with slices and then with low/high arguments to avoid copying, and use bisect_left and insort from the standard library.

knowledge_points.title: Recursive search on halves

knowledge_points.title: Slices copy: pass low and high instead

knowledge_points.title: bisect_left finds where an item is or would go

import bisect
items = [3, 8, 12, 19, 25]
i = bisect.bisect_left(items, 19)

import bisect
items = [3, 8, 12]

topics.title: Bubble sort: swapping neighbours
topics.summary: Sort a list in place by repeatedly swapping out-of-order neighbours until a pass makes no swaps, and explain why that is O(n²) in the worst case and O(n) on sorted input.

knowledge_points.title: One pass: swap neighbours that are out of order
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the list after one pass; fix a pass that raises IndexError by using range(len(nums)).

knowledge_points.title: Repeat passes until nothing is swapped
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of bubble sort; fill in where the flag is reset and set.

knowledge_points.title: Trace the passes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# [5, 1, 4, 2]
# after pass 1: [1, 4, 2, 5]
# after pass 2: [1, 2, 4, 5]
# pass 3: no swaps, stop
After pass k the k largest items are in their final places at the end.

topics.title: Selection sort: choosing the smallest each time
topics.summary: Sort a list by repeatedly finding the smallest remaining item and swapping it into the next position, trace the growing sorted prefix, and count its always-O(n²) comparisons.

knowledge_points.title: Find the position of the smallest item from i onward
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]
i = 2
smallest = i
for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
    if nums[j] < nums[smallest]:
        smallest = j
print(smallest, nums[smallest])  # 4 13
Track the position of the smallest so far, not its value, so it can be swapped afterwards.

knowledge_points.title: Swap it into place, for every position
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of selection sort; fill in the swap.

knowledge_points.title: The sorted part grows by one each pass
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]
# i=0: [10, 29, 14, 37, 13]
# i=1: [10, 13, 14, 37, 29]
# i=2: [10, 13, 14, 37, 29]
# i=3: [10, 13, 14, 29, 37]
After pass i, positions 0..i hold the smallest items in order and never change again.

knowledge_points.title: Always about n²/2 comparisons
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 5
print(n * (n - 1) // 2)  # 10 comparisons, even for an already sorted list
The inner loop always scans the whole rest, so selection sort is O(n²) in every case, but makes at most n swaps.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute comparison counts for given n; compare best cases of selection and bubble sort.

topics.title: Insertion sort: sliding each item into place
topics.summary: Sort a list by inserting each item into the sorted part before it, shifting larger items right, guard the shift with j >= 0, and see why it is fast on nearly sorted input.

knowledge_points.title: Insert one item into a sorted prefix
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [2, 5, 9, 4]   # the first three are sorted
key = nums[3]
j = 2
while j >= 0 and nums[j] > key:
    nums[j + 1] = nums[j]
    j -= 1
nums[j + 1] = key
print(nums)  # [2, 4, 5, 9]
Larger items shift one place right until the gap is where key belongs.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace j and the list while one item is inserted.

knowledge_points.title: Do it for every item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def insertion_sort(nums):
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        key = nums[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and nums[j] > key:
            nums[j + 1] = nums[j]
            j -= 1
        nums[j + 1] = key
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
insertion_sort(nums)
print(nums)  # [1, 2, 5, 9]
Start at index 1: a one-item prefix is already sorted.
knowledge_points.practice: Reorder the lines of insertion sort; predict the list after each outer pass.

knowledge_points.title: Bug: the j >= 0 guard must come first
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 1]
key, j = nums[1], 0
nums[1] = nums[0]
j -= 1
print(j, nums[j])  # -1 3: without j >= 0 the loop would compare with the last item
nums[-1] is valid Python, so a missing guard gives wrong results instead of an error. and stops before nums[j] once j >= 0 is False.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the missing or misordered guard in insertion sort code; predict what the buggy version does.

knowledge_points.title: Fast on nearly sorted lists
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Sorted input: each key is compared once and nothing shifts, n - 1 comparisons: O(n).
Reversed input: key i shifts past all i earlier items, about n²/2 shifts: O(n²).
That is why insertion sort is used for small or nearly sorted data, even inside Python's own sorted().
knowledge_points.practice: Count shifts for given inputs; choose the best algorithm for nearly sorted data.

topics.title: Merging two sorted lists
topics.summary: Combine two sorted lists into one sorted list in O(n) by repeatedly taking the smaller front item and then adding the leftovers.

knowledge_points.title: Compare the fronts, take the smaller
knowledge_points.worked_example:
left, right = [1, 4, 9], [2, 3, 10]
merged = []
if left[0] <= right[0]:
    merged.append(left[0])
else:
    merged.append(right[0])
print(merged)  # [1]

left, right = [1, 4, 9], [2, 3, 10]

while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
